chapters.title: Accounting Principles: Concepts, Conventions and Standards
chapters.scope: The ten basic concepts and four conventions that every set of accounts rests on, and the Indian standards that turn them into rules.

blocks.title: Entity, money measurement and cost
blocks.html:
Ravi opens a kirana store with ₹5,00,000 of his savings. A month later he pays ₹5,000 of his daughter’s school fee from the shop’s cash. Is that a cost of running the shop?

In plain wordsThe accounts treat the business as one person and its owner as another. They record only what has a money value, at the price actually paid.

Exam definitionBusiness entity concept: a business is a unit separate from its owner, and its books record its transactions, not the owner’s. Money measurement concept: only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. Cost concept: an asset is recorded at its acquisition cost.

Entity. Ravi’s ₹5,00,000 is not the shop’s own money. The shop owes it to him, and the books call it capital. When he takes ₹5,000 for the school fee, the shop’s cash falls to ₹4,95,000 and so does his capital. The fee is not an expense of the shop; it is a drawing.

Money measurement. The shop’s books will record the refrigerator, the stock and the rent. They will not record that its best employee is unhappy, that a rival opened nearby, or that Ravi’s regular customers trust him. These matter, but a rupee value cannot be put on them reliably.

Cost. Ravi buys a refrigerator for ₹40,000. The books show ₹40,000, even if a new one costs ₹46,000 next year or he could sell this one for ₹30,000. Cost is a fact on a bill; the other values are opinions.

ConceptWhat it saysIn Ravi’s books
Business entityThe business is separate from its owner₹5,000 for the school fee is a drawing, not an expense
Money measurementRecord only what has a money valueRefrigerator, stock and rent are recorded; staff morale is not
CostRecord assets at what was paidRefrigerator at ₹40,000 whatever it is worth later

Don’t confuse the accounting entity with the legal one. A sole proprietor is not legally separate from his shop; he is personally liable for its debts. His accounts still keep the two apart. A company is separate in both law and accounts.

Where it breaks. In years of inflation, cost understates old assets: a building bought in 1990 for ₹10 lakh may now be worth ₹2 crore, yet the books show ₹10 lakh less depreciation. Under Ind AS 16 a company may choose to revalue some assets. Money measurement leaves out people, brands and customer trust, which are often a firm’s main strengths.

For exams. Be ready to say which concept a case shows: private spending from business cash is entity; an unrecorded labour dispute is money measurement; a machine shown at purchase price is cost.

Entity: the owner stands apart. Money: only what a rupee can measure. Cost: what you paid.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why cost wins. Accountants have four ways to value an asset: what it cost, what it would cost now, what it would sell for, and the present value of what it will earn. Cost is objective, because anyone can check the bill. The others need guesses, and the last needs a guess about the future.

A decision. A friend asks you to join as a partner in his workshop and shows you accounts that value a 20-year-old lathe at its purchase price less depreciation. Which of the other three values would you ask for before putting in money, and why?

Links. Year-end adjustments (Chapter 2 in this unit) shows how cost is spread over an asset’s life as depreciation.

blocks.title: Dual aspect and the accounting equation
blocks.html:
Ravi buys ₹2,00,000 of goods on credit from a supplier. No cash has moved, yet the books must change. How do they stay in balance?

In plain wordsEvery transaction has two sides. The books record both, so what the business has always equals what it owes.

Exam definitionDual aspect concept: every transaction has a twofold effect, recorded as a debit and an equal credit. This gives the accounting equation, Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

Follow Ravi’s store through four transactions. After each one, assets equal liabilities plus capital.

TransactionCashFurnitureStockTotal assetsCreditorsCapital
1. Ravi puts in ₹5,00,000₹5,00,000––₹5,00,000–₹5,00,000
2. Buys furniture for ₹1,00,000 in cash₹4,00,000₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000–₹5,00,000
3. Buys goods for ₹2,00,000 on credit₹4,00,000₹1,00,000₹2,00,000₹7,00,000₹2,00,000₹5,00,000
4. Pays the supplier ₹1,50,000₹2,50,000₹1,00,000₹2,00,000₹5,50,000₹50,000₹5,00,000

Each line shows a different kind of change. In 2, one asset rises and another falls. In 3, an asset and a liability rise together. In 4, an asset and a liability fall together. A fourth kind moves between liabilities: if the supplier agrees to turn the ₹50,000 owed into a loan, creditors fall and loans rise.

In debit and credit. Transaction 3 is written as a journal entry: Debit Stock ₹2,00,000; Credit Creditors ₹2,00,000. Debit increases an asset or an expense. Credit increases a liability, capital or an income.

Don’t think a balanced set of books is a correct one. The two sides can agree and still be wrong. If Ravi books the school fee as a shop expense, debits and credits still match; the mistake is in the choice of account. Chapter 2 lists the errors a trial balance cannot catch.

Where it breaks. The equation holds by construction, so it proves nothing about whether each entry is true. Only checking against bills, bank statements and stock counts does that.

For exams. Write the equation, say which two accounts a given transaction touches, and state whether each rises or falls.

Two sides, one amount: debit equals credit, assets equal what is owed.

Go deeper for practitioners

Capital moves too. Profit raises capital and drawings lower it, so the full equation is Assets = Liabilities + opening capital + profit − drawings. This is why the profit and loss account and the balance sheet always agree.

A decision. At month end Ravi’s assets are ₹5,50,000 and creditors ₹50,000, so capital is ₹5,00,000. Yet he feels he has earned something. What is missing from this picture, and which statement will show it?

blocks.title: Going concern and periodicity
blocks.html:
A textile mill in Surat has run for 60 years and expects to run for 60 more. Its owners want to know every year whether it is doing well. They cannot wait for the mill to close before they find out.

In plain wordsThe accounts assume the business will carry on, so assets are valued for use, not for a quick sale. Its long life is cut into yearly slices so progress can be measured.

Exam definitionGoing concern concept: the enterprise is assumed to continue in operation for the foreseeable future, with no intention or need to liquidate or materially curtail its operations. Periodicity concept: the life of a business is divided into equal accounting periods.

Going concern. The mill buys a machine for ₹7,00,000 and pays ₹70,000 more for transport and installation. Under the cost concept the machine is recorded at ₹7,70,000. If it will last ten years with no scrap value, the books charge ₹77,000 a year. They do not write it down to what a scrap dealer would pay this month, because the mill is not selling it; it is using it.

Periodicity. In India most businesses report for the financial year, 1 April to 31 March, and a company must close its books on 31 March, with narrow exceptions. A year is usual, but a firm may also report each quarter. Equal periods let owners compare this year with last year.

Don’t read going concern as a promise that the firm will survive. It is a starting assumption. If the firm is likely to close, the accounts must be prepared on a different basis, and the basis must be disclosed. Auditors report a “material uncertainty related to going concern” when there is real doubt.

Where it breaks. Cutting life into years forces estimates: how long a machine will last, which sales belong to March. These estimates are judgements, and a year’s profit depends on them. Short periods can also push managers to favour this year’s profit over long-term value.

For exams. Going concern explains why fixed assets are depreciated, not shown at sale value. Periodicity explains why accounts are made every period, and why it is the base for matching revenue with cost.

Going concern: the business goes on, so spread the cost. Periodicity: cut the life into years.

Go deeper for practitioners

Cut-off. A period’s edge matters. A lorry load delivered on 31 March is this year’s sale; the same load delivered on 2 April belongs to next year. Firms and auditors watch the days around year-end because moving a sale across the line moves a year’s profit.

A decision. A distributor is close to a lender’s profit target on 28 March and a large order could be dispatched early. What do the concepts say about when the sale belongs, and what would you tell your owner?

Links. Realisation, accrual and matching (next concept) set the rule for which sales and costs fall inside a period.

blocks.title: Realisation, accrual and matching
blocks.html:
A furniture maker in Jaipur delivers a sofa set worth ₹1,20,000 on 28 March. The customer pays on 10 April. Which year’s income is it? And what about the timber that went into it?

In plain wordsCount a sale when you deliver, not when you are paid. Count a cost when you use it, not when you pay. Then set each sale against the costs that earned it.

Exam definitionRealisation concept: revenue is recognised when it is earned, not necessarily when cash is received. Accrual concept: revenues and costs are recognised as they are earned or incurred, not as money is received or paid, and are reported in the period they relate to. Matching concept: the expenses of a period are matched with the revenue they helped earn.

A year in Meera’s shop. Meera buys 1,000 sarees at ₹800. She sells 800 at ₹1,200, taking ₹8,00,000 in cash and leaving ₹1,60,000 due from customers. Her rent is ₹10,000 a month; she has paid for 11 months.

ItemCash basisAccrual basis
Sales₹8,00,000 received₹9,60,000 (800 sarees at ₹1,200; ₹1,60,000 still due)
Cost of goods₹8,00,000 paid for 1,000 sarees₹6,40,000 for the 800 sold; ₹1,60,000 of stock unsold
Rent₹1,10,000 paid (11 months)₹1,20,000 (12 months; ₹10,000 still owed)
ResultCash −₹1,10,000Profit ₹2,00,000

The cash view shows a loss of ₹1,10,000. The accrual view shows a profit of ₹2,00,000. The accrual view is the better guide to how the shop did. It counts all ₹9,60,000 of sales, it counts the cost of the 800 sarees sold and carries the other 200 forward as stock, and it counts a full year of rent.

Revenue − expenses = profit: ₹9,60,000 − ₹6,40,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹2,00,000

Matching. Some costs link directly to sales, like the saree’s purchase price. Others link to time, like rent, and are charged to the period they cover. Both are matched to the period in which the revenue is counted. This is what creates prepaid and outstanding expenses and accrued and unearned income at year-end.

Don’t confuse profit with cash. Meera’s profit is ₹2,00,000 but her cash fell by ₹1,10,000. The difference is ₹1,60,000 owed by customers, ₹1,60,000 tied up in unsold stock, less ₹10,000 of rent not yet paid. This is why a profitable business can still run out of cash.

Where it breaks. Accrual needs judgement about when a sale is earned, how much will be returned and how many customers will pay. Firms can bring sales forward to look better. Ind AS 115 sets a five-step test for revenue, recognised as control passes to the customer; AS 9 was the older rule.

For exams. Know Revenue − Expenses = Profit, and be able to turn a cash record into an accrual profit.

Earn it, count it. Use it, count it. Match cost to the sale.

Go deeper for practitioners

Realisation, three tests. Revenue is usually counted when the seller has delivered, the price is fixed or can be fixed, and collection is reasonably sure. If any fails, as with goods sold on trial, the sale waits.

A decision. A software firm sells a three-year licence for ₹36 lakh on 1 January and gets paid up front. If the year ends on 31 March, how much is this year’s revenue, and where does the rest sit on the balance sheet? (Think of it as service delivered over time.)

Links. The cash flow statement (Chapter 6) starts from accrual profit and converts it back to cash.

blocks.title: The four conventions
blocks.html:
A company changes how it depreciates its machines and its profit jumps by ₹40 lakh. Nothing in the business has changed. Should readers be told? And should the company be free to change every year?

In plain wordsConventions are the habits accountants follow so that accounts are honest and can be compared. Four matter most: tell everything, stay consistent, be cautious, and ignore trivia.

Exam definitionAccounting conventions are customs and practices that have been followed over a long period and guide the preparation of accounts: disclosure, consistency, conservatism and materiality.

ConventionThe ruleAn example
DisclosureShow all material information users needContingent liabilities appear in the notes; companies follow the Schedule III format; SEBI requires listed firms to disclose more
ConsistencyUse the same methods year after yearA depreciation method is not changed without a reason, and the change and its effect are disclosed
Conservatism (prudence)Anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible lossesStock at the lower of cost and net realisable value; a provision for doubtful debts
MaterialityDetail only what could change a user’s decisionA calculator bought for ₹900 is charged as an expense in full, though it lasts years

Conservatism, worked. A trader’s stock cost ₹2,40,000. If its net realisable value (what it can be sold for, less selling costs) falls to ₹2,10,000, the books value it at ₹2,10,000 and show a loss of ₹30,000 now. If its value rises to ₹2,70,000, the books keep it at ₹2,40,000. The gain of ₹30,000 appears only when the stock is sold. Losses are recognised early; gains wait.

Don’t confuse concepts with conventions. Concepts, like entity and accrual, are basic assumptions about how accounting is structured. Conventions, like consistency and materiality, are accepted practices that shape how information is presented. Textbooks use the two words loosely, so give the example if asked.

Don’t treat conservatism as permission to understate profit. Prudence means taking care not to overstate. Deliberately understating profit, by building hidden reserves, is also a misstatement.

Where it breaks. Conservatism can make accounts biased downward, and gains and losses are treated unevenly. Consistency can lock in an outdated method. Materiality has no fixed rupee limit; it depends on the size of the firm and the nature of the item.

For exams. Recall the phrase for conservatism and the stock rule: lower of cost and net realisable value (AS 2 and Ind AS 2).

Disclose it. Keep it consistent. Provide for losses, not for gains. Ignore the trivial.

Go deeper for practitioners

Prudence in the framework. The IASB’s 2018 Conceptual Framework put prudence back, defining it as the exercise of caution under uncertainty, without allowing deliberate understatement. It sits beside neutrality: information should be even-handed.

A decision. A firm’s receivables include ₹30 lakh from one customer that is six months overdue and disputing the bill. The auditor says provide in full; the owner says wait. Which convention is at stake, and what evidence would settle it?

blocks.title: Accounting standards in India
blocks.html:
Two companies buy identical machines. One writes the cost off in five years, the other in twenty. Their profits are not comparable. Standards exist so that similar events are accounted for in the same way.

In plain wordsAn accounting standard is an official rule for how a particular item must be recorded, measured, shown and explained. India has two sets: the older Accounting Standards (AS) and the newer Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), which follow international ones.

Exam definitionAccounting standards are authoritative statements, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) and notified by the Central Government under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, on the treatment and disclosure of accounting items. Ind AS are converged with IFRS.

Who makes them. ICAI recommends a standard. The Central Government notifies it as rules, after consulting the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). The Accounting Standards are notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, first issued in 2006. The Ind AS are in the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015.

Who follows which. Ind AS apply to listed companies and to larger unlisted ones, decided by net-worth limits. Other companies follow AS. The limits have been revised, so check the current notification before you rely on a number.

TopicAccounting StandardIndian Accounting Standard
InventoriesAS 2, Valuation of InventoriesInd AS 2, Inventories
Cash flowsAS 3, Cash Flow StatementsInd AS 7, Statement of Cash Flows
RevenueAS 9, Revenue RecognitionInd AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers
Property, plant and equipmentAS 10Ind AS 16
LeasesAS 19Ind AS 116
Earnings per shareAS 20Ind AS 33
Consolidated statementsAS 21Ind AS 110
Financial instrumentsNo full standard is notifiedInd AS 109 (and Ind AS 107 for disclosures)
Fair value measurementNoneInd AS 113

Don’t mix the two numbering systems. AS 3 and Ind AS 7 both deal with cash flows; AS 9 and Ind AS 115 both deal with revenue. An exam question that gives only a number needs you to know which set it comes from.

Where it breaks. Ind AS bring in fair values and expected-loss models, which need more judgement and make profits less steady. Smaller firms find the full set costly to apply, which is why they keep AS.

For exams. Recall: AS 2 inventories, AS 3 cash flows, AS 9 revenue, AS 19 leases, AS 20 earnings per share; Ind AS 109 financial instruments, 110 consolidation, 113 fair value, 115 revenue, 116 leases.

Links. Chapter 3 takes Ind AS and IFRS further: the phases of adoption, how they differ from IFRS and a longer list of standards.

ICAI recommends, the Government notifies. AS for most, Ind AS for the large and listed.

Go deeper for practitioners

The convergence idea. Ind AS follow IFRS closely, with a few carve-outs for Indian conditions. Convergence lets foreign investors read Indian accounts without translating them. Carve-outs are the points where India chose a different treatment.

A decision. Your company’s net worth is close to the Ind AS limit and may cross it next year. List three things you would do this year to prepare, such as training, systems and a trial set of Ind AS accounts.

pairings.modern: Periodic accounts to a fixed form
text: Kauṭilya’s accounts office (akṣapaṭala) keeps registers for every department, fixes when and how accounts are to be presented, and sets penalties for officials who fail to present them. Accounts at fixed times and in a fixed form are the habit that periodicity and disclosure later made routine.

chapters.title: Preparation of Financial Statements
chapters.scope: The five parts of a company’s final accounts, the steps from first entry to finished statements, and the year-end adjustments.

blocks.title: What the final accounts contain
blocks.html:
A bank is deciding whether to lend ₹50 lakh to Sundaram Textiles. It asks for the company’s accounts. What does each statement tell the banker that the others do not?

In plain wordsA company’s final accounts are a set of statements: one photograph of what it has and owes on a day, and several accounts of what happened over the year.

Exam definitionThe financial statements of a company comprise the Balance Sheet, the Statement of Profit and Loss, the Cash Flow Statement, the Statement of Changes in Equity, and the Notes to Accounts.

StatementWhat it showsTimeKey relation
Balance SheetWhat the company has and owesOn one dateAssets = Liabilities + Equity
Statement of Profit and LossHow much it earned and spentOver a periodIncome − Expenses = Profit
Cash Flow StatementWhere cash came from and wentOver a periodClosing cash = Opening cash + Net change
Statement of Changes in EquityHow owners’ funds movedOver a periodOpening + Profit + Shares issued − Dividends = Closing
Notes to AccountsPolicies, details and disclosuresAttached to all the aboveExplains figures; adds contingent liabilities

Here are Sundaram Textiles’ statements for the year ended 31 March, in one set of figures. Look for the same numbers turning up in different statements.

ParticularsAmount

Total expenses₹9,40,000

Share capital₹6,00,000Property, plant and equipment₹6,50,000
Other equity₹5,30,000Inventories₹2,40,000
Long-term borrowings₹2,00,000Trade receivables₹2,20,000
Trade payables₹1,50,000Cash and cash equivalents₹3,70,000
Total₹14,80,000Total₹14,80,000
Cash flowAmountChanges in equityAmount
Operating activities₹2,60,000Opening balance₹8,00,000
Investing activities−₹1,80,000Profit for the year+₹2,10,000
Financing activities+₹1,70,000Shares issued+₹1,50,000
Net increase in cash₹2,50,000Dividends paid−₹30,000
Opening cash₹1,20,000Closing balance₹11,30,000
Closing cash₹3,70,000

The links. Cash on the balance sheet, ₹3,70,000, is the closing cash in the cash flow statement. Equity on the balance sheet, ₹6,00,000 + ₹5,30,000 = ₹11,30,000, is the closing balance in the statement of changes in equity. The profit of ₹2,10,000 flows into equity. But the company earned ₹2,10,000 and cash rose by ₹2,50,000: profit and cash are different things.

Schedule III. The Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the layout. Division I is for companies following AS, Division II for those following Ind AS. Both list equity and liabilities on one side, assets on the other, each split into current and non-current.

Don’t confuse the balance sheet with the profit and loss account. A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date. The profit and loss account is a film of a whole year. One shows position, the other performance.

Where it breaks. Statements look back, rest on estimates, and say nothing about the strength of the team or the brand. A company can also choose when to record some items so that a snapshot looks better than the year was.

For exams. Name the five parts, say which one answers which question (position, performance, cash, owners’ funds, details), and give the equation for each.

Position at a date, performance over a period, cash by activity, owners’ funds, and notes.

Go deeper for practitioners

Other comprehensive income. Under Ind AS some gains and losses, such as revaluation of certain assets, bypass the profit and loss account and go to “other comprehensive income”. They still change equity, which is why the statement of changes in equity has a line for them.

A decision. Sundaram’s profit is ₹2,10,000 but cash rose by ₹2,50,000, and its receivables are ₹2,20,000. As the banker, which statement would you read first to see whether it can repay a loan, and what would you ask?

blocks.title: From first entry to finished statements
blocks.html:
A shopkeeper has a bag of bills, a bank passbook and a notebook. How does that become a balance sheet an auditor can sign?

In plain wordsAccounting follows a fixed route. Each deal is written down, sorted into accounts, checked, adjusted at year-end, and only then turned into statements.

Exam definitionThe accounting cycle is the sequence of recording transactions in journals, posting them to ledger accounts, preparing a trial balance, making adjustments, preparing an adjusted trial balance, drawing up financial statements, and obtaining review and approval.

A month in Ravi’s store. Four transactions in April show steps 1 to 4.

DateDebitCreditAmount
1 AprCashCapital₹5,00,000
3 AprFurnitureCash₹1,00,000
5 AprPurchasesGupta Traders (a creditor)₹2,00,000
20 AprGupta TradersCash₹1,50,000

Ledger. Each entry is posted to the accounts it touches. The cash account gets ₹5,00,000 on the debit side, and ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,50,000 on the credit side, leaving a balance of ₹2,50,000.

AccountDebitCredit
Cash₹2,50,000
Furniture₹1,00,000
Purchases₹2,00,000
Capital₹5,00,000
Gupta Traders₹50,000
Total₹5,50,000₹5,50,000

The totals agree, so the books are arithmetically sound. At year-end come the adjustments (next concept), a fresh trial balance, and then the statements. The board approves them, and the statutory auditor reports on them before they go to shareholders.

Don’t confuse the journal, the ledger and the trial balance. The journal lists transactions in date order. The ledger groups them by account. The trial balance is a check on the ledger, not a statement for outsiders.

Where it breaks. A matching trial balance does not mean the books are right. See “Go deeper” for the errors it cannot catch.

For exams. Know the order of the steps, and which are done during the year and which at the end.

Record, journal, ledger, test, adjust, retest, report, approve.

Go deeper for practitioners

Four errors the trial balance misses. (1) Omission: a whole transaction is not recorded. (2) Commission: an amount goes to the wrong account of the same kind, such as to Gupta Traders instead of Gupta Brothers. (3) Principle: a transaction is put in the wrong class, such as treating a capital item as an expense. (4) Compensating: two errors of equal size on opposite sides cancel out.

A decision. Ravi’s accountant paid ₹20,000 for repairing the shop’s roof and debited it to “Buildings”. The trial balance still agrees. Which error is this, and how does it change the year’s profit?

blocks.title: Year-end adjustments: depreciation, accruals and provisions
blocks.html:
On 31 March a shop’s books are still missing three things. The machine is a year older. March’s electricity has not been billed. And some customers will probably never pay. If nothing is done, the profit is wrong.

In plain wordsBefore the statements are drawn, the books are corrected for things that have happened but not yet been written down: wear on assets, costs owed or paid in advance, and debts unlikely to be collected.

Exam definitionAdjusting entries bring the accounts in line with the accrual and matching concepts. Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life. A provision is an amount set aside against a known loss or liability whose size is uncertain.

Four adjustments, worked. The shop has a machine that cost ₹7,70,000 with a ten-year life and no scrap value, rent of ₹10,000 a month, a one-year insurance premium of ₹24,000 paid on 1 January, and debtors of ₹5,00,000 of which it expects 4% to go bad.

AdjustmentEntryAmountEffect on profit
Depreciation (straight-line)Debit Depreciation; credit Accumulated depreciation₹77,000−₹77,000
Rent for March, unpaid (outstanding)Debit Rent; credit Outstanding rent₹10,000−₹10,000
Insurance paid in advance (prepaid): the full premium was charged when paid, and 9 of 12 months are still unexpiredDebit Prepaid insurance; credit Insurance expense₹18,000+₹18,000
Provision for doubtful debts: 4% of ₹5,00,000Debit Bad debts; credit Provision for doubtful debts₹20,000−₹20,000
Net effect on profit−₹89,000

Depreciation methods. Straight-line charges ₹77,000 every year. The written-down value method charges a fixed percentage of what is left: at 10%, year one is ₹77,000 and year two is 10% of ₹6,93,000, which is ₹69,300. The machine’s book value after year one is ₹6,93,000.

Accruals and deferrals. An outstanding expense is incurred but unpaid, and is added. A prepaid expense is paid in advance for a later period, and is removed from this year’s cost. Accrued income is earned but not received; unearned income is received for a later period.

Don’t confuse a provision with a reserve. A provision is charged against profit for a loss or liability that is known or likely. A reserve is profit kept back, such as a general reserve, and is not a cost. Don’t confuse depreciation with saving cash, either: depreciation spreads cost and sets no cash aside.

Where it breaks. Depreciation rests on estimates of life and scrap value. A longer life gives a higher profit. Schedule II of the Companies Act lists useful lives for companies, but management still judges the method and the condition of the asset. Provisions can be used to move profit between years.

For exams. Write the journal entries. Remember that depreciation, outstanding expenses and provisions lower profit, and prepaid expenses and accrued income raise it.

Wear it, owe it, prepay it, doubt it.

Go deeper for practitioners

Revenue and capital. A repair keeps an asset working and is a cost of the year. A new roof that lasts twenty years adds to the asset and is capitalised, then depreciated. Putting one in the other’s place is an error of principle and moves profit by the whole amount.

A decision. A firm is one month from year-end and could delay ₹8 lakh of repairs into next year, or reclassify them as an addition to the building. Which choice moves profit up, which concept limits it, and what would an auditor ask for?

pairings.modern: The statement of income and expenditure
text: The Arthaśāstra lists the heads of the state’s revenue: fortified cities, countryside, mines, irrigation works, forests, herds and trade routes. It pairs them with an accounts office that records income and expenditure. A profit and loss account is that kind of statement. The passage describes a state’s revenue, not a company’s profit, so the link is a reading.

blocks.title: Why accounting standards matter, and who makes them
blocks.html:
A company invoices ₹50 lakh of sales on 28 March but ships the goods on 3 April. One accountant counts the sale in this year, another in the next. Both think they are right. Without a common rule, two honest firms report different profits for the same facts.

In plain wordsAn accounting standard is an authoritative rule on how an item must be recorded, measured, shown and explained, so that all firms treat the same event the same way.

Exam definitionAccounting standards prescribe the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of transactions in financial statements. They form the core of generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and bind the entities required to follow them.

ReasonWhat it gives
Uniformity and comparabilityStatements prepared the same way, so investors can compare firms and years
Transparency and reliabilityA common accounting language, which reduces ambiguity
Global alignmentInd AS are converged with IFRS, so cross-border investors can read Indian accounts
Fraud preventionA standard format and treatment makes manipulation harder
Guidance for auditorsClear yardsticks against which accounts are checked

Two sets in India. The older Accounting Standards (AS) are notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006. The newer Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) follow the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and are notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015. A company follows one set or the other, depending on its size and listing.

Convergence, not adoption. India converged with IFRS: it aimed for harmony and kept the right to modify a standard where Indian conditions called for it. That is why Ind AS are numbered like IFRS (Ind AS 16 for IAS 16) but are not word-for-word copies.

Who does what. The Accounting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) prepares the drafts. An independent body advises the Government: the notes name the National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards (NACAS), and under the Companies Act 2013 this role now goes through the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) notifies the standards as rules.

Don’t say Ind AS replaced AS everywhere. India has had two sets side by side. Companies covered by Ind AS follow it, and all others continue under AS. The line between them is drawn by net worth and listing, and it has been revised more than once.

Where it breaks. Standards cannot cover every case, so they leave room for judgement, and judgement can be bent. Detailed rules can also push firms to arrange deals to fit the letter and not the spirit. Compliance with a standard is not the same as a fair picture.

For exams. Know the five reasons, the two sets, the meaning of convergence, and the roles of ICAI, NFRA and the MCA.

ICAI drafts, NFRA advises, MCA notifies; convergence is harmony, not copying.

Go deeper for practitioners

The numbering clue. Ind AS follow the IFRS numbering, so Ind AS 7 corresponds to IAS 7 (cash flows). The older AS follow their own series, so AS 3 is the cash flow standard. A question that gives only a number needs you to know which series it belongs to.

A decision. A group has one listed company and three small unlisted subsidiaries. What problems could arise from the two sets of standards, and who would need to reconcile them?

blocks.title: Ind AS, IFRS and the phases of adoption
blocks.html:
A foreign investor is comparing an Indian company with a firm in Europe. If both follow IFRS-based rules, the investor can read them side by side. That was the promise behind converging Indian standards with IFRS.

In plain wordsIFRS are global standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). Ind AS are India’s version of them, notified by the Government and applied by a defined list of companies in phases.

Exam definitionIFRS are accounting standards developed by the IASB, under the oversight of the IFRS Foundation, to bring uniformity, transparency and comparability to financial reporting across borders. Ind AS are standards converged with IFRS and notified by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

IFRSInd AS
What it isGlobal standards of the IASBIndia’s converged version of IFRS
Issued byThe IASB; governed by the IFRS FoundationNotified by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, on the advice of ICAI and NFRA
Where usedRequired or permitted in well over 100 countriesIndia only
Statement of complianceAn explicit statement of compliance is requiredAlso required: Ind AS 1 asks for an explicit statement of compliance
Balance sheet formatA current and non-current split is required, but no single fixed layoutThe layout is set by Schedule III of the Companies Act (Division II for Ind AS)
StatementsFinancial position, profit and loss, changes in equity, cash flows, and notesBalance sheet, profit and loss, changes in equity, cash flow, and notes with accounting policies

Phased adoption. Ind AS were brought in step by step, by net worth and listing, starting from 1 April 2016.

PhaseFromWho
I1 April 2016Companies with a net worth of ₹500 crore or more, and listed or soon-to-be-listed companies in that group
II1 April 2017Listed companies not in Phase I, and unlisted companies with a net worth of ₹250 crore or more but under ₹500 crore
IIIFrom 1 April 2018NBFCs, in steps by net worth, on a timetable set with their regulator
VoluntaryFrom 1 April 2015Companies not covered above may choose to adopt Ind AS

Holding, subsidiary, associate and joint venture companies of a covered company are drawn in too. Banks and insurers follow timetables set with the Reserve Bank of India and the insurance regulator, and not the general rule.

Don’t trust a net-worth number from a study note. The thresholds above are the original scheme. The rules have been amended, and the notes that describe them are often out of date. The current limits are in the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended. Treat any number here as a guide to the idea.

Where it breaks. Ind AS bring in more fair values and forward-looking estimates than the older rules. That makes accounts more informative but also more dependent on judgement, and profit can move more from year to year. Small companies find the cost of complying heavy, which is why they keep the simpler AS.

For exams. Know who issues IFRS and who notifies Ind AS, the idea of phases and the first date, and the difference between IFRS and Ind AS in format and body.

IASB makes IFRS; the Ministry notifies Ind AS; companies join by phase.

Go deeper for practitioners

Carve-outs. Where India departed from IFRS, the departures are called carve-outs. Examples have included treatment of some foreign exchange items and of certain financial instruments. A set of accounts under Ind AS may therefore not carry an unqualified claim of full IFRS compliance. Check the notes to the accounts for that statement.

A decision. A company’s net worth has crossed the Ind AS threshold. What would you want in place before the first year of Ind AS, and who in the company should lead the change?

blocks.title: The main standards and their counterparts
blocks.html:
An exam question says ‘Ind AS 36’ and asks what it covers. Another says ‘AS 29’. Knowing which standard deals with which topic, and which old standard matches which new one, is the whole task.

In plain wordsMost Ind AS have an older AS on the same topic. The topic is the link between them, even though the content differs.

Exam definitionEach Indian Accounting Standard corresponds in subject to an Accounting Standard notified under the 2006 Rules, though the Ind AS follow IFRS and may differ in scope, measurement and disclosure.

Ind ASTopicAS on the same topic
Ind AS 1Presentation of financial statementsAS 1 (disclosure of accounting policies; narrower)
Ind AS 2Inventories: lower of cost and net realisable valueAS 2
Ind AS 7Statement of cash flowsAS 3
Ind AS 8Accounting policies, changes in estimates and errorsAS 5
Ind AS 10Events after the reporting periodAS 4
Ind AS 12Income taxesAS 22
Ind AS 16Property, plant and equipmentAS 10
Ind AS 19Employee benefitsAS 15
Ind AS 20Government grants and assistanceAS 12
Ind AS 21Effects of changes in foreign exchange ratesAS 11
Ind AS 23Borrowing costsAS 16
Ind AS 24Related party disclosuresAS 18
Ind AS 33Earnings per shareAS 20
Ind AS 34Interim financial reportingAS 25
Ind AS 36Impairment of assetsAS 28
Ind AS 37Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assetsAS 29
Ind AS 38Intangible assetsAS 26
Ind AS 115Revenue from contracts with customersAS 9
Ind AS 116LeasesAS 19

Others with no neat pair. Ind AS 109 (financial instruments) and Ind AS 113 (fair value measurement) have no full counterpart among the AS. Ind AS 41 (agriculture) has none either. Ind AS 110 covers consolidated statements (AS 21 is the older one), and Ind AS 27 covers separate statements.

What the IFRS side looks like. The IFRS series is numbered IFRS 1 onwards, and sits next to the older International Accounting Standards (IAS). Examples are IFRS 9 (financial instruments), IFRS 15 (revenue from contracts with customers), IFRS 16 (leases) and IFRS 17 (insurance contracts). New standards are issued from time to time, so a list is only a snapshot.

Mind the errors in common notes. Some notes print the wrong pairs: they set Ind AS 27 against AS 21 (AS 21 is the consolidated statements standard, and consolidation is Ind AS 110), and Ind AS 41 against AS 14, which is about amalgamations. They also describe IFRS 9 as ‘replacing IFRS 7’. In fact IFRS 7 still deals with disclosure for financial instruments, and IFRS 9 replaced the older IAS 39. Always check against the standard itself.

Where it breaks. A table of pairs hides differences. Ind AS 115 and AS 9 both deal with revenue, yet Ind AS 115 uses a five-step model that can recognise revenue at a different time. Ind AS 116 puts most leases on the balance sheet, which AS 19 did not for operating leases.

For exams. Memorise the pairs that are asked most: Ind AS 2 and AS 2, Ind AS 7 and AS 3, Ind AS 16 and AS 10, Ind AS 33 and AS 20, Ind AS 36 and AS 28, Ind AS 37 and AS 29, Ind AS 115 and AS 9, Ind AS 116 and AS 19.

Same topic, different number, different content.

Go deeper for practitioners

Impairment as a worked idea. Both Ind AS 36 and AS 28 test whether an asset is carried at more than it could recover. If a machine is in the books at ₹40 lakh but can recover only ₹32 lakh, the difference of ₹8 lakh is an impairment loss. The standard sets how to estimate what can be recovered.

A decision. Your company leases 40 vehicles on five-year terms. Under AS 19 they were mostly off the balance sheet. What changes under Ind AS 116, and which ratios of Chapter 4 would move?

chapters.title: Ratio Analysis: Liquidity, Profitability, Activity and Solvency
chapters.scope: How to read the financial statements through four families of ratios, with one company’s figures worked end to end.

blocks.title: What ratio analysis does
blocks.html:
A bank has two borrowers. One earns ₹4,20,000 a year, the other ₹9,00,000. Which is safer? The answer depends on how much each owns, owes and sells, and a ratio puts those figures side by side.

In plain wordsA ratio divides one figure from the accounts by another, so firms of different sizes, or one firm in different years, can be compared.

Exam definitionRatio analysis is the technique of evaluating financial performance by studying relationships between items in the financial statements. Ratios are grouped into liquidity, profitability, activity (turnover) and solvency ratios.

One company for every ratio. This chapter uses Kaveri Auto Parts, a small maker in Coimbatore. Every ratio that follows comes from these figures.

Statement of profit and lossAmountBalance sheetAmount
Net sales (₹40,00,000 on credit)₹50,00,000Shareholders’ equity₹24,00,000
Cost of goods sold₹35,00,000Long-term borrowings₹8,00,000
Gross profit₹15,00,000Current liabilities (₹2,00,000 of them borrowings; trade payables ₹5,00,000)₹8,00,000
Operating profit (EBIT)₹7,00,000Total equity and liabilities₹40,00,000
Interest₹1,00,000Non-current assets₹22,00,000
Profit before tax₹6,00,000Inventory₹8,00,000
Tax at 30%₹1,80,000Debtors₹6,00,000
Net profit₹4,20,000Cash and cash equivalents₹4,00,000

The opening balances are inventory ₹6,00,000, debtors ₹4,00,000 and creditors ₹4,00,000. Kaveri has 1,00,000 shares, and its market price is ₹63.

How to read a ratio. A number means little alone. Compare it three ways: with the firm’s own past years (trend), with similar firms (inter-firm), and with a standard such as 2:1 for the current ratio.

Don’t treat a rule of thumb as a law. The ‘ideal’ current ratio of 2:1 and quick ratio of 1:1 are conventions. A supermarket that sells for cash and pays suppliers on credit runs safely on less. What matters is the pattern in your industry.

Where it breaks. Ratios use past, accrual-based figures, and firms use different accounting policies. A year-end snapshot can be dressed up. Inflation distorts comparisons over time. A ratio shows that something looks odd, not why.

For exams. Know the four families and one formula for each ratio, and which statement each figure comes from.

Liquidity, profitability, activity, solvency: short-term, earning, efficiency, long-term.

Go deeper for practitioners

The consistent numerator and denominator. A ratio should divide like by like. A profit earned over a year is divided by an average of the balance sheet figures, or at least by the year-end figure used the same way every time. A comparison breaks if one firm uses averages and the other the closing figure.

A decision. A supplier offers Kaveri two months’ credit if it raises its purchases by ₹10 lakh. Which family of ratios would you look at first, and what would you want to see?

blocks.title: Uses, types and limits of ratios
blocks.html:
Firm A earns ₹50,000 on sales of ₹5,00,000. Firm B earns ₹1,00,000 on sales of ₹50,00,000. B’s profit is twice as large, but is B the more efficient? Set against sales, A keeps 10% and B keeps 2%.

In plain wordsRatios are grouped by where the figures come from (income statement, balance sheet or both) and by what they test (liquidity, profitability, activity, solvency). They help, but they have limits.

Exam definitionA traditional classification divides ratios into income statement ratios, balance sheet ratios and composite ratios. A functional classification, by purpose, gives liquidity, profitability, turnover (activity) and leverage (solvency) ratios.

TypeBoth figures come fromExample
Income statement ratioThe statement of profit and lossGross profit ratio: gross profit ÷ sales
Balance sheet ratioThe balance sheetCurrent ratio: current assets ÷ current liabilities
Composite ratioOne from eachDebtors turnover: credit sales (profit and loss) ÷ debtors (balance sheet)

What the analysis is for. It shows the present and likely future earning power of a business, the efficiency of the whole firm and of its departments, its short-term and long-term solvency, and it makes comparison with other firms easy.

UserInterestRatios
Short-term creditorsWill I be paid on the due date?Liquidity ratios
Long-term lenders and investorsIs the firm sound over the long run?Solvency (capital structure) ratios
ManagementOverall profitability and efficiencyProfitability and activity ratios
ShareholdersEarnings and dividendsEarnings per share, return on equity

Advantages. Ratios make statements easier to read. They show trends from year to year, which helps forecasting. They support control and decision-making, and they show the links between different parts of the business.

Limitations. Ratios leave out qualitative factors, such as the quality of management or the loyalty of customers, because they are built on money figures. A single year’s ratio says little, and trends over several years say more. And if the accounts are defective or the firm leaves things out on purpose, the ratios will be wrong in the same way.

Don’t treat a good ratio as proof of a good firm. A ratio can be right and still mislead. Different firms use different accounting policies, and a year-end snapshot can be arranged to look better. Use ratios to find questions to ask, and look for the answer in the business.

Where it breaks. Ratios are only as good as the data. Inflation distorts comparisons across years. A firm that is a mix of several industries has no single sensible benchmark.

For exams. Know both classifications with an example of each, and be ready to list advantages and limitations.

Where the figures come from, and what the ratio tests.

Go deeper for practitioners

Common-size statements. A useful way to spot changes is to express every item as a percentage of sales, or of total assets. Items that move out of line from one year to the next show where to look, before any ratio is chosen.

A decision. A bank sees a firm whose ratios have all improved this year. What would you ask to be sure the improvement is real?

blocks.title: Liquidity ratios
blocks.html:
Kaveri has ₹18,00,000 in current assets and ₹8,00,000 in current liabilities. Can it pay everything it owes in the next year, and could it pay this week if suppliers called their bills?

In plain wordsLiquidity ratios check whether a firm has enough cash and near-cash to pay what it owes in the next twelve months.

Exam definitionLiquidity ratios measure the ability of the firm to meet short-term obligations out of current assets. They include the current ratio, the quick (acid-test) ratio and the cash ratio.

RatioFormulaConvention
Current ratioCurrent assets ÷ Current liabilitiesAbout 2 : 1
Quick (acid-test) ratio(Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilitiesAbout 1 : 1
Cash ratio(Cash + Cash equivalents) ÷ Current liabilitiesDepends on the business

Kaveri’s figures.

Current ratio = ₹18,00,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 2.25 : 1
Quick ratio = (₹18,00,000 − ₹8,00,000) ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 1.25 : 1
Cash ratio = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 0.50 : 1

Kaveri passes the usual tests. Even without selling any stock it has ₹1.25 of liquid assets for each ₹1 due. Half the amount due could be met from cash alone.

Don’t confuse the quick ratio with the current ratio. The quick ratio leaves out inventory because stock can take months to turn into cash, and may sell below cost. A firm with a healthy current ratio but a weak quick ratio is relying on its stock being sold.

Where it breaks. A very high liquidity ratio is not good news by itself. It may mean cash lying idle, slow-moving stock or debtors who do not pay. Ratios taken on one day can also be improved by year-end window dressing, such as paying creditors just before the date.

Two related points. Strictly, quick assets also leave out prepaid expenses, and quick liabilities leave out a bank overdraft that is a permanent part of financing. The stock-working capital ratio is closing stock ÷ working capital: ₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 = 0.8, so stock is 80% of Kaveri’s working capital. The nearer it is to 100%, the more working capital rests on selling stock.

For exams. Learn the three formulas and the 2 : 1 and 1 : 1 benchmarks, and remember that higher means better short-term payment capacity, up to a point.

Current: all current assets. Quick: leave out stock. Cash: only cash.

Go deeper for practitioners

Working capital. The difference between current assets and current liabilities, here ₹10,00,000, is the money tied up in running the business each day. The fund flow statement (Chapter 5) follows this figure.

A decision. A distributor’s current ratio falls from 2.2 to 1.4 in a year as sales boom and inventory builds. Is it in trouble? What would you check in the quick ratio, the debtors’ days and the supplier terms before you decide?

blocks.title: Profitability ratios
blocks.html:
Kaveri sold ₹50,00,000 and kept ₹4,20,000. Is that a good year? It depends on what it earned from each rupee of sales, and from each rupee its owners and lenders put in.

In plain wordsProfitability ratios show how much profit a firm makes out of its sales, its assets and its owners’ money.

Exam definitionProfitability ratios assess the ability of the firm to generate profit relative to sales, assets or equity: gross profit ratio, net profit ratio, return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE).

RatioFormula
Gross profit ratio(Gross profit ÷ Net sales) × 100
Net profit ratio(Net profit ÷ Net sales) × 100
Return on assets (ROA)(Net profit ÷ Total assets) × 100
Return on equity (ROE)(Net profit ÷ Shareholders’ equity) × 100
Gross profit ratio = ₹15,00,000 ÷ ₹50,00,000 × 100 = 30%
Net profit ratio = ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹50,00,000 × 100 = 8.4%
Return on assets = ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹40,00,000 × 100 = 10.5%
Return on equity = ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹24,00,000 × 100 = 17.5%

Out of every ₹100 of sales Kaveri keeps ₹30 after the cost of goods and ₹8.4 at the end. Each ₹100 of assets earns ₹10.5, and each ₹100 the owners have in the business earns ₹17.5. ROE is higher than ROA because part of the assets are paid for with debt.

A market ratio. Earnings per share is net profit ÷ number of shares: ₹4,20,000 ÷ 100,000 = ₹4.20. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is the share price ÷ earnings per share: ₹63 ÷ ₹4.20 = 15. It shows how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of earnings. A higher ratio signals more confidence in future earnings.

Don’t mix up the denominators. ROA divides by all assets, ROE only by the owners’ funds. Gross and net profit ratios both divide by net sales. If a question says ‘return on capital employed’ it uses yet another denominator, so read it.

Where it breaks. A high margin on few sales can earn less than a thin margin on many. Profit is an accrual figure and can be moved between years. ROE can be raised by borrowing more, which also raises the risk; a high ROE with high debt is not a safe one.

For exams. Recall the four formulas and the sequence gross profit, net profit, return on assets, return on equity. The P/E ratio is often asked.

Gross, net, assets, equity: the denominator changes from sales to what is invested.

Go deeper for practitioners

Two routes to the same return. Net profit ratio × asset turnover = ROA: 8.4% × 1.25 = 10.5%. A firm can earn a high return by a high margin (a jeweller) or by turning assets fast (a supermarket). Asking which route a firm uses explains its strategy.

A decision. Two rival firms both earn a 12% ROE. One has debt of 0.2 times equity; the other 1.5 times. Which would you rather lend to, and why?

blocks.title: Operating ratio, capital employed and earnings per share
blocks.html:
Kaveri’s gross profit is ₹15,00,000 but its operating profit is ₹7,00,000. Where did ₹8,00,000 go, and how much does it earn on the long-term money in the business?

In plain wordsThe operating ratio shows what share of sales is eaten by the cost of goods and running expenses. The return on capital employed shows how well the firm’s long-term funds are used.

Exam definitionOperating ratio = (Cost of goods sold + Operating expenses) ÷ Sales × 100. Operating profit ratio = Operating profit ÷ Sales × 100. Return on capital employed (ROCE) = Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100, where capital employed = Debt + Equity, or Fixed assets + Working capital.

Operating ratio = (₹35,00,000 + ₹8,00,000) ÷ ₹50,00,000 × 100 = 86%
Operating profit ratio = ₹7,00,000 ÷ ₹50,00,000 × 100 = 14%

The two add to 100%. Of each ₹100 of sales, ₹86 goes on running the business and ₹14 is operating profit, before interest and tax. A lower operating ratio means more is left to pay interest, tax and dividends and to build reserves.

Capital employed = Equity ₹24,00,000 + Long-term borrowings ₹8,00,000 = ₹32,00,000
ROCE = ₹7,00,000 ÷ ₹32,00,000 × 100 = 21.9%

The same ₹32,00,000 is also fixed assets ₹22,00,000 plus working capital ₹10,00,000. Kaveri earns about ₹22 before interest and tax on each ₹100 of long-term money. Compared with a borrowing rate of 10%, that is a good margin.

Earnings per share, again. EPS is the profit available to equity shareholders divided by the number of equity shares. Profit available is profit after tax less any preference dividend. If Kaveri also paid ₹20,000 of preference dividend, EPS would be (₹4,20,000 − ₹20,000) ÷ 100,000 = ₹4.00.

Don’t read a fall in EPS as a fall in profit. If Kaveri issued one bonus share for every four held, its shares would rise from 100,000 to 125,000. Profit is unchanged, but EPS falls from ₹4.20 to ₹3.36. The firm has not become less profitable; its profit is just spread over more shares.

Where it breaks. ROCE uses profit before interest and tax, so it can look good for a firm that pays heavy interest. The definition of capital employed differs between books, so say which one you use. The operating ratio treats all costs as one lump, and does not show which cost rose.

For exams. Learn the formulas, and that operating ratio and operating profit ratio add to 100%. Know that ROCE is also called return on investment (ROI).

Operating ratio plus operating profit ratio makes 100.

Go deeper for practitioners

Compare ROCE with the cost of borrowing. If ROCE is higher than the interest rate, extra borrowing can raise the return to owners. If it is lower, borrowing makes things worse. This is the logic of leverage, and Chapter 16 returns to it.

A decision. A firm’s ROCE is 9% and its bank loan costs 11%. Should it expand using the loan? What would you check first?

blocks.title: Activity (turnover) ratios
blocks.html:
Kaveri holds ₹8,00,000 of stock and is owed ₹6,00,000 by customers. If both sit for a year, the money is idle. How fast do they turn into sales and cash?

In plain wordsActivity ratios show how many times a firm turns its stock, debtors or assets into sales in a year. A higher figure usually means money is used more efficiently.

Exam definitionActivity (turnover) ratios measure how efficiently a business uses its assets to generate sales: inventory turnover, debtors turnover, creditors turnover and asset turnover.

RatioFormulaWhat it measures
Inventory turnoverCost of goods sold ÷ Average inventoryHow fast stock moves
Debtors turnoverNet credit sales ÷ Average accounts receivableHow efficiently dues are collected
Creditors turnoverNet credit purchases ÷ Average accounts payableHow quickly suppliers are paid
Asset turnoverNet sales ÷ Total assetsSales from each rupee of assets

Averages. Kaveri’s average inventory is (₹6,00,000 + ₹8,00,000) ÷ 2 = ₹7,00,000. Average debtors are ₹5,00,000, and average creditors ₹4,50,000. Credit purchases are cost of goods sold plus the rise in stock, ₹35,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹37,00,000, taking all purchases as on credit.

Inventory turnover = ₹35,00,000 ÷ ₹7,00,000 = 5 times, or 73 days of stock
Debtors turnover = ₹40,00,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 = 8 times, or 45.6 days to collect
Creditors turnover = ₹37,00,000 ÷ ₹4,50,000 = 8.22 times, or 44.4 days to pay
Asset turnover = ₹50,00,000 ÷ ₹40,00,000 = 1.25 times

Kaveri collects in about 46 days and pays in about 44 days, so customers and suppliers are treated about the same. Stock sits for 73 days. To cut the cash tied up, it would first work on stock.

Don’t use the wrong figure on top. Inventory turnover uses cost of goods sold, not sales, because stock is valued at cost. Debtors turnover uses credit sales only, since cash sales never create a debtor. Using total sales makes collection look faster than it is.

Fixed assets turnover. Net sales ÷ net fixed assets shows how many rupees of sales each rupee of fixed assets produces. Taking Kaveri’s non-current assets of ₹22,00,000 as its net fixed assets, it is ₹50,00,000 ÷ ₹22,00,000 = 2.27 times. A higher figure means the plant is used harder.

A worked question. Opening stock is ₹58,000, closing stock is ₹58,000 + ₹4,000 = ₹62,000, sales are ₹6,40,000, and gross profit is 25% on cost. Cost of goods sold is the sales × 100/125 = ₹5,12,000. Average stock is ₹60,000. Stock turnover = ₹5,12,000 ÷ ₹60,000 = 8.53 times. The catch is that 25% on cost is only 20% of sales.

The average payment period. 365 ÷ creditors turnover. It is the average credit period used: for Kaveri about 44 days. (Some books misprint this as debtors turnover; the formula uses the creditors figure.)

Where it breaks. A high turnover is not always better: very fast stock turnover may mean frequent stock-outs, and slow payment of creditors may harm supplier trust. Seasonal firms need averages over several points in the year, not two balance-sheet dates.

For exams. Remember the four formulas and the line ‘higher turnover generally means efficient use’. Convert turnover to days by dividing 365 by the ratio.

Stock on cost, debtors on credit sales, creditors on credit purchases, assets on sales.

Go deeper for practitioners

The cash cycle. Stock days plus debtors days minus creditors days is the time between paying for materials and receiving cash from customers. For Kaveri it is 73 + 45.6 − 44.4 ≈ 74 days of its own money tied up. Every day cut releases cash.

A decision. A retailer’s debtors’ days are 3 and its creditors’ days are 60, while a machine builder’s are 90 and 45. Which of the two needs more working capital for each rupee of sales, and what does that say about its lenders’ view of it?

blocks.title: Solvency ratios
blocks.html:
Kaveri owes ₹10,00,000 to lenders. Whether that is comfortable depends on how much the owners have in the business and on whether profits cover the interest.

In plain wordsSolvency ratios show whether a firm can carry its debt over the long run, by comparing debt with what the owners put in and with what the firm earns.

Exam definitionSolvency ratios measure the long-term financial stability of a firm and its ability to meet long-term obligations: the debt-to-equity ratio, the debt ratio and the interest coverage ratio.

RatioFormulaReading
Debt-to-equityTotal debt ÷ Shareholders’ equityLower means less financial risk
Debt ratioTotal debt ÷ Total assetsShare of assets paid for by debt
Interest coverageEBIT ÷ Interest expenseHigher means interest is safer
Debt-to-equity = ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹24,00,000 = 0.42
Debt ratio = ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹40,00,000 = 0.25, or 25%
Interest coverage = ₹7,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 7 times

Lenders have put in 42 paise for every rupee the owners have, and they finance a quarter of the assets. Operating profit is seven times the interest, so a fall of up to six-sevenths in operating profit would still leave the interest covered.

Don’t confuse the debt ratio with debt-to-equity. The first divides by total assets, the second by owners’ equity only. Debt-to-equity is always the larger of the two (unless there is no debt). Many sources also differ on what to count as debt, so always check whether short-term borrowings are included.

Three more tests. The proprietary ratio is shareholders’ funds ÷ total assets: ₹24,00,000 ÷ ₹40,00,000 = 0.6, so owners paid for 60% of the assets. The capital gearing ratio is fixed-interest and fixed-dividend funds ÷ equity funds: ₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹24,00,000 = 0.33. The total assets to debt ratio is total assets ÷ long-term debt: ₹40,00,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 5 times, so each rupee of long-term debt is covered five times over by assets.

Which debt? Some books take only long-term debt: ₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹24,00,000 = 0.33, against 0.42 when short-term borrowings are included. Many treat 2 : 1 as the most that is prudent, except for a few businesses. Always say which definition you use.

Where it breaks. Debt is not bad in itself: borrowing at 10% to earn 18% raises the owners’ return. What matters is whether the firm earns well above its interest rate and has steady profits. A cyclical firm with the same ratios is riskier than a steady one.

For exams. Recall the three formulas and that lower debt ratios mean lower risk, higher interest coverage means safer interest.

Debt against owners’ money, debt against assets, profit against interest.

Go deeper for practitioners

Leverage cuts both ways. If Kaveri’s operating profit fell by 40%, interest would still be a fixed ₹1,00,000, so net profit would fall by more than 40%. That magnifying effect is why capital structure choices matter, and why Chapter 16 looks at the theories.

A decision. A lender is asked to extend ₹10 lakh to Kaveri. Using the ratios in this chapter, which three would you put in a one-paragraph note to the credit committee, and what would you ask about before approving?

chapters.title: Fund Flow Statement
chapters.scope: What ‘funds’ means, how a transaction changes working capital, and how to prepare the schedule and the statement of sources and applications.

blocks.title: Funds and the flow of funds
blocks.html:
A firm shows a profit of ₹1,40,000, yet it bought a machine, repaid a loan and paid a dividend. Where did the money come from, and where did it go? A fund flow statement answers that, but first it needs an exact meaning of ‘funds’.

In plain wordsIn this statement ‘funds’ means working capital, the money tied up in running the business each day. It does not mean cash. A ‘flow’ is any change in that working capital.

Exam definitionA fund flow statement shows the sources from which funds were obtained and the uses to which they were put between two balance sheet dates. Funds here means net working capital: current assets less current liabilities.

The rule. Working capital changes only when a transaction touches one current account and one non-current account. If both accounts are current, working capital merely shifts inside itself. If both are non-current, it is not touched.

TransactionAccounts touchedFlow of funds?
Equity shares issued for cashCash (current), Share capital (non-current)Yes, a source
Machine bought for cashMachine (non-current), Cash (current)Yes, an application
Goods bought on creditStock and creditors (both current)No
Creditors paid in cashCreditors and cash (both current)No
Machine bought by issuing sharesMachine and share capital (both non-current)No
Debentures redeemed by issuing sharesDebentures and share capital (both non-current)No

Where each account sits. Current: stock, debtors, bills receivable, cash, prepaid expenses, short-term investments, creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, dividend payable and short-term loans. Non-current: share capital, reserves, the profit and loss balance, debentures, long-term loans, fixed assets, goodwill and long-term investments.

Don’t confuse funds with cash. Cash is only one part of working capital. Selling goods on credit raises working capital but not cash, and paying a creditor lowers cash without changing working capital. That difference is why the cash flow statement (Chapter 6) was added.

Where it breaks. The treatment of some items varies by textbook. A provision for tax, or a proposed dividend, may be treated as a non-current appropriation or as a current liability. Follow the treatment the question states. The statement also ignores non-cash tactics that move funds without a visible entry.

For exams. State the meaning of funds as working capital, and decide each transaction by whether it crosses between current and non-current.

Cross the line, move the funds; stay in the box, no flow.

Go deeper for practitioners

The statement’s limits. Because working capital lumps stock, debtors and cash together, the statement hides a squeeze in cash. A firm can show a rising working capital and still be unable to pay wages, if the rise is in slow stock. The cash flow statement closes that gap, and the cash flow of Chapter 6 for the same firm shows it.

A decision. A firm buys a plot by issuing shares of the same value to the seller. Does this appear in a fund flow statement? Would it appear in a cash flow statement? What does your answer say about when each statement is the right tool?

blocks.title: Schedule of changes in working capital
blocks.html:
Narmada Plastics’ working capital was ₹2,50,000 last March and is ₹3,00,000 this March. The first job is to see which current items made up that ₹50,000 rise.

In plain wordsThe schedule lists each current asset and current liability for two years, finds the change in each, and totals the effect on working capital.

Exam definitionThe schedule of changes in working capital is prepared from current assets and current liabilities alone. An increase in a current asset or a decrease in a current liability increases working capital; a decrease in a current asset or an increase in a current liability decreases it.

ItemLast yearThis yearRaises working capitalLowers working capital
Current assets
Stock₹1,20,000₹1,60,000₹40,000
Debtors₹80,000₹1,10,000₹30,000
Cash and bank₹1,10,000₹1,00,000₹10,000
Total current assets₹3,10,000₹3,70,000
Current liabilities
Creditors₹60,000₹70,000₹10,000
Working capital₹2,50,000₹3,00,000
Total effect₹70,000₹20,000
Net increase in working capital₹50,000

The last two columns show the effect on working capital, not the direction of the item. A rise in creditors sits in the right-hand column because it lowers working capital.

The four rules.

  • A rise in a current asset raises working capital.
  • A fall in a current asset lowers it.
  • A rise in a current liability lowers it.
  • A fall in a current liability raises it.

Here stock rises by ₹40,000 and debtors by ₹30,000, which add ₹70,000. Cash falls by ₹10,000, and creditors rise by ₹10,000, which together take away ₹20,000. The net is ₹50,000.

₹70,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹50,000 increase

Don’t mix up the direction for liabilities. A liability that grows is money a supplier is lending, which sounds like a gain but is a claim to be paid soon. It reduces the net current assets left over, so working capital falls. Most mistakes in this schedule come from reversing this one rule.

Where it breaks. The schedule only explains the total. It does not say why working capital rose. That is the job of the statement of sources and applications, and the two must agree to the rupee.

For exams. Present the schedule first, with last year’s and this year’s balances side by side, and carry its net result to the funds statement as a check.

Assets up, working capital up. Liabilities up, working capital down.

Go deeper for practitioners

Is a rise always good? Working capital here rose partly because stock and debtors grew by ₹70,000 while cash fell by ₹10,000. Growing stock and debtors can be a sign of a firm selling more, or of goods that will not sell and customers who will not pay. The ratios of Chapter 4 help to decide which.

A decision. A firm’s working capital rises by ₹5 lakh, all of it in stock. Its cash fell. What would you want to know before calling that an improvement?

blocks.title: Statement of sources and applications of funds
blocks.html:
Working capital rose by ₹50,000. Which long-term decisions caused it? Narmada raised money, sold a machine, bought another, repaid a loan and paid a dividend, and each of these needs to be placed on one side or the other.

In plain wordsThe statement lists the long-term money that came in (sources) and the long-term money that went out (applications). The gap between them is the change in working capital.

Exam definitionA statement of sources and applications of funds is prepared from changes in non-current accounts and funds from operations. Total sources less total applications equals the net increase or decrease in working capital shown by the schedule.

Funds from operations. This is the main internal source. Start with profit and add back charges that used no working capital (depreciation, goodwill written off, losses on sale of fixed assets), then deduct any gains on such sales, which are shown separately. Here, taxes are paid in the year they are charged.

Profit before tax ₹2,00,000 + Depreciation ₹40,000 − Tax paid ₹60,000 = Funds from operations ₹1,80,000
Sources of fundsAmountApplications of fundsAmount
Funds from operations₹1,80,000Purchase of machinery₹1,70,000
Issue of equity shares₹1,00,000Repayment of long-term loan₹40,000
Sale of old machine₹20,000Dividend paid₹40,000
Net increase in working capital₹50,000
Total₹3,00,000Total₹3,00,000

The sources total ₹3,00,000 and the applications ₹2,50,000. The balance, ₹50,000, is the increase in working capital, and it agrees with the schedule of the previous concept.

Usual sources. Funds from operations, issue of shares or debentures, long-term borrowing, and the sale of fixed assets or long-term investments. Usual applications. Purchase of fixed assets or investments, redemption of debentures or preference shares, repayment of long-term loans, payment of dividends, and a net loss from operations.

Don’t treat depreciation as a source of funds. Depreciation is added back only because it was deducted without using any working capital. The cash does not come from depreciation; it comes from sales. Adding it back stops profit from being understated as a measure of funds from operations.

Where it breaks. The statement does not report how cash itself moved, so it cannot show a looming shortage. In practice, companies covered by the accounting standards present a cash flow statement; the fund flow statement is a management and exam tool, so check the current rules for any firm.

For exams. Show the working: funds from operations first, then sources and applications, then the check that the difference equals the schedule’s result.

Long-term in is a source, long-term out is an application; the gap is working capital.

Go deeper for practitioners

Reading the story. Narmada financed its ₹1,70,000 machine from operations (₹1,80,000) and new shares (₹1,00,000), while paying off ₹40,000 of loan and distributing ₹40,000. It grew working capital by funding it from profit and equity, not debt. That is the kind of conclusion the statement is built to support.

A decision. If Narmada had funded the same machine by short-term borrowing instead of shares, what would have happened to working capital, and why would a lender worry?

chapters.title: Cash Flow Statement
chapters.scope: How a firm reports the cash that came in and went out, in the three activities, by the direct and the indirect method, and how it differs from the fund flow statement.

blocks.title: Cash and the three activities
blocks.html:
A firm can show a profit and still be unable to pay its wages. A cash flow statement shows what profit hides: how much cash actually came in, where it came from, and where it went.

In plain wordsA cash flow statement lists the cash that came in and went out during the year, sorted into three kinds of activity. It explains why the cash balance changed.

Exam definitionThe cash flow statement reports the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents for a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. Cash comprises cash in hand and demand deposits; cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value.

ActivityWhat it coversTypical inflowsTypical outflows
OperatingThe firm’s principal revenue-producing activitiesCash from customers, fees, commission, royaltiesPayments to suppliers and employees, income tax
InvestingBuying and selling long-term assets and other investmentsSale of fixed assets or investments, interest and dividends received, repayment of loans givenPurchase of fixed assets or investments, loans given
FinancingChanges in owners’ capital and borrowingsIssue of shares or debentures, loans takenRepayment of loans, interest paid, dividends paid

Worked sorting. A cash sale of goods, payment to a raw-material supplier, salaries and income tax are operating. Buying a machine, and interest received on investments, are investing. Issuing shares at a premium, paying a dividend, interest on debentures and repaying a long-term loan are financing.

Non-cash transactions are left out. Buying a machine by issuing shares, or redeeming debentures by issuing shares, uses no cash, so it is not in the statement, although it should be disclosed elsewhere.

Same item, different class. The purchase of shares is an operating cash flow for a share broker, and an investing one for a manufacturer. The class depends on the firm’s business.

Don’t confuse profit with cash from operations. Profit is on the accrual basis and counts sales when made, not when paid. Cash from operations counts only money actually received and paid, so a firm that sells on long credit shows profit but little cash.

Where it breaks. Classification of interest and dividends differs between the Indian standards and between kinds of firm. The text above follows the usual treatment under AS 3 for a non-financial company. Check which standard (AS 3 or Ind AS 7) and which firm the question is about, since Ind AS 7 allows choices of classification in some cases.

For exams. Be able to sort items into the three activities, define cash equivalents, and say which items are excluded as non-cash.

Operating: the business. Investing: the assets. Financing: the owners and lenders.

Go deeper for practitioners

What each section tells you. Strong operating cash with large investing outflow suggests a firm that is growing out of its own earnings. Weak operating cash covered by new borrowing in financing is a warning: the business is not paying for itself.

A decision. A company reports a profit of ₹50 lakh, an operating cash flow of −₹10 lakh and new loans of ₹60 lakh. A lender is asked to extend the loan. What do these three figures say together?

blocks.title: Direct and indirect method
blocks.html:
The investing and financing sections are simple lists. The difficulty is the operating section, which can be built in two ways that must give the same answer.

In plain wordsThe direct method adds up the cash received from customers and subtracts the cash paid out. The indirect method starts with profit and corrects it for non-cash items and changes in stock, debtors and creditors.

Exam definitionIn the direct method, major classes of gross cash receipts and payments are disclosed. In the indirect method, profit before tax is adjusted for non-cash items and for changes in working capital to arrive at cash generated from operations. Only the operating section differs between the two methods.

The figures. Narmada Plastics has sales of ₹10,00,000, profit before tax of ₹2,00,000, depreciation of ₹40,000 and income tax paid of ₹60,000. Over the year its stock rose by ₹40,000, its debtors rose by ₹30,000 and its creditors rose by ₹10,000.

LineAmount
Profit before tax₹2,00,000
Add: Depreciation (non-cash)₹40,000
Operating profit before working capital changes₹2,40,000
Less: Increase in stock−₹40,000
Less: Increase in debtors−₹30,000
Add: Increase in creditors+₹10,000
Cash generated from operations₹1,80,000
Less: Income tax paid−₹60,000
Net cash from operating activities₹1,20,000
LineAmount
Cash received from customers (₹10,00,000 less the ₹30,000 rise in debtors)₹9,70,000
Cash paid to suppliers and employees (₹7,60,000 of costs, plus the ₹40,000 rise in stock, less the ₹10,000 rise in creditors)−₹7,90,000
Cash generated from operations₹1,80,000
Less: Income tax paid−₹60,000
Net cash from operating activities₹1,20,000

Both methods give the same result, because they are two routes through the same transactions. The rules for the adjustments follow one idea: money that is stuck in current assets is not cash, and money not yet paid out on liabilities is still in the bank.

ChangeEffect on cash from operationsWhy
Increase in a current asset (stock, debtors)SubtractCash is tied up in it
Decrease in a current assetAddCash has been released
Increase in a current liability (creditors)AddPayment has been put off
Decrease in a current liabilitySubtractCash has been paid out

Don’t add depreciation to the cash flow as if it were a receipt. Depreciation was deducted in arriving at profit without any cash leaving. It is added back only to undo that deduction. Losses on the sale of assets are added back, and gains deducted, for the same reason: the cash from the sale is shown in investing.

Where it breaks. The direct method needs cash records by category that many firms do not keep, and the indirect method hides the gross receipts. Most companies present the indirect method. Whether the direct method is required is a matter of the standard and the type of entity, so check the current notification.

For exams. Know both layouts, the rule for each current item, and the fact that only the operating section changes between the methods.

Asset up, cash down. Liability up, cash up.

Go deeper for practitioners

Working the tax. Tax in the P&L may differ from tax paid, because of a provision. Only the tax actually paid belongs in the statement. Here the two are the same by assumption (₹60,000 charged and paid in the year); with a provision, adjust by the change in the provision.

A decision. A firm’s sales rise 30% but its debtors’ days rise from 40 to 70. Using the indirect method as a guide, what happens to its operating cash flow, and what could the firm do about it?

blocks.title: Fund flow versus cash flow
blocks.html:
Narmada’s working capital rose by ₹50,000 and its cash fell by ₹10,000, in the same year. Both statements are right. They measure different things.

In plain wordsThe fund flow statement explains why working capital changed. The cash flow statement explains why cash changed. A firm can do well on the first and badly on the second.

Exam definitionA funds flow statement analyses changes in the working capital position between two balance sheet dates. A cash flow statement analyses the movement of cash and cash equivalents between the same dates, classified into operating, investing and financing activities.

ActivityItemAmount
OperatingCash generated from operations₹1,80,000
Income tax paid−₹60,000
Net cash from operating activities₹1,20,000
InvestingPurchase of machinery−₹1,70,000
Sale of old machine+₹20,000
Net cash used in investing activities−₹1,50,000
FinancingIssue of equity shares+₹1,00,000
Repayment of long-term loan−₹40,000
Dividend paid−₹40,000
Net cash from financing activities+₹20,000
