Net change in cash−₹10,000
Cash at the start of the year₹1,10,000
Cash at the end of the year₹1,00,000
FeatureFund flow statementCash flow statement
What it explainsChange in working capitalChange in cash and equivalents
Starting pointSchedule of current assets and liabilitiesOpening cash balance
Debtors and stockPart of funds: their increase raises working capitalTheir increase absorbs cash
Shows by activity?No: sources and applicationsYes: operating, investing, financing
Narmada’s resultWorking capital up ₹50,000Cash down ₹10,000

Reconciling the two. Working capital rose by ₹50,000. Stock and debtors added ₹70,000, and neither is cash. Cash itself fell by ₹10,000, and the extra creditors took off another ₹10,000. The funds statement shows a year of growth; the cash statement shows that the firm’s cash went down, because the growth was tied up in stock and debtors.

Don’t treat the two as rivals. The fund flow statement shows how long-term money was raised and used, and the cash flow statement shows whether the firm can pay its bills. A good analysis uses both. In practice, companies covered by the standards present the cash flow statement; the fund flow statement is a management and exam tool.

Where it breaks. A cash flow statement for one year says little about the next. Cash can be changed by timing, such as paying creditors early. Look at several years, and at operating cash against profit.

For exams. Remember the difference in one line: funds are working capital, cash is cash. Know that the statements start from the same balance sheets and, for the same firm, agree on the long-term items.

Funds for the structure, cash for the survival.

Go deeper for practitioners

Free cash. A rough test of a firm’s strength is operating cash flow less the cash spent on fixed assets. Narmada generated ₹1,20,000 and spent ₹1,70,000 on machinery, taking ₹20,000 from the sale. Without the new shares its cash would have fallen from ₹1,10,000 to nil.

A decision. A bank sees two firms with the same rise in working capital. One has rising operating cash and the other has falling operating cash. Which would it lend to, and why can the funds statement alone not tell them apart?

pairings.classic: the channel of income and the channel of outflow
text: The Kuṟaḷ says that even a narrow income does no harm as long as the outflow is not wider than the inflow. A cash flow statement tests exactly that for a business: whether cash coming in covers cash going out. The couplet speaks of a ruler’s or household’s treasury, not of a company, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Though the channel of income be narrow, there is no harm if the channel of outflow is not wider.” ஆகாறு அளவிட்டி தாயினுங் கேடில்லை போகாறு அகலாக் கடை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 478

chapters.title: Cost Accounting and the Cost Sheet
chapters.scope: What cost accounting is for, how costs are sorted, and how a cost sheet builds up from prime cost to selling price.

blocks.title: Cost accounting and its purpose
blocks.html:
A weaver in Madurai sells a saree for ₹2,400 and is told that is a fair price. Is it? She cannot know until she knows what one saree costs her to make, and that is the question cost accounting answers.

In plain wordsCost accounting records what things cost to make and sell, sorts those costs, and helps the owner control them and set a price.

Exam definitionCost accounting is the process of recording, classifying, analysing and controlling costs in order to determine the cost per unit, improve efficiency and support managerial decision-making.

Its objectives. Cost control and cost computation, pricing and decision-making, valuing inventory, studying profitability by product, and budgeting and performance evaluation.

BasisCost accountingFinancial accounting
PurposeInternal control and decision-makingExternal reporting and compliance
UsersManagementInvestors, lenders, regulators
DataHistorical and estimatedMainly historical
RulesMostly set by management’s needsSet by law and standards
ReportingAs often as management wants itPeriodic, quarterly and annually

Methods and techniques. A method is chosen to fit how the product is made: job costing for one-off orders such as furniture, batch costing for garments made in lots, process costing for continuous output such as cement, contract costing for long projects such as a building, and activity-based costing, which spreads overhead by what causes it. A technique is a way of using the figures: standard costing, marginal costing, budgetary control and uniform costing.

Don’t say cost accounting is free of law. Cost accounting has no single statute for all firms. But the Companies Act 2013 lets the Government require cost records and a cost audit for notified classes of company, so some firms must keep them. Check the notification for the sector.

Where it breaks. Costs that cannot be traced to a product, such as head-office salaries, are shared out by a rule, and a different rule gives a different cost. Estimates of future cost can be wrong, and the effort of keeping detailed records must be worth the benefit.

For exams. Know the meaning, the objectives, the comparison with financial accounting and the list of methods against techniques.

Methods follow the product; techniques follow the question.

Go deeper for practitioners

Cost, price and value. A cost is what the firm gives up to make something. A price is what the customer pays. Cost accounting tells you the first and sets a floor under the second. It does not say what the customer will pay.

A decision. A tailor takes both one-off wedding orders and batches of school uniforms. Which costing method would you use for each, and why?

blocks.title: Types and elements of cost
blocks.html:
A bakery’s rent is the same whether it bakes 100 loaves or 1,000. The flour is not. A cost that behaves differently needs a different treatment, and the first step is to sort them.

In plain wordsCosts are sorted by how they behave (fixed, variable or a mix) and by whether they can be traced to a product (direct or indirect). The elements are material, labour, expenses and overheads.

Exam definitionA fixed cost remains constant irrespective of output. A variable cost changes directly with the level of production. A semi-variable cost has both fixed and variable components. A direct cost is traceable to a specific product or job; an indirect cost is not.

TypeMeaningExample
Fixed costConstant, whatever the outputRent, salaries
Variable costChanges directly with outputRaw materials
Semi-variable costPart fixed, part variableElectricity, repairs
Direct costTraceable to a product or jobDirect labour
Indirect costNot directly traceableOffice expenses

A semi-variable cost, worked. An electricity bill has a fixed charge of ₹2,000 and ₹5 for each unit of power used. At 400 units the bill is ₹4,000; at 1,000 units it is ₹7,000. The fixed part never moves, and the variable part moves with use.

ElementWhat it covers
MaterialRaw materials used in production, direct and indirect
LabourDirect wages of workers and indirect wages such as supervision
ExpensesDirect expenses (special tools) and indirect expenses (rent)
OverheadsFactory, administrative and selling and distribution overheads
Prime cost = Direct material + Direct labour + Direct expenses
Total cost = Prime cost + Overheads

Don’t confuse fixed with direct. ‘Fixed’ and ‘variable’ describe how a cost changes with output. ‘Direct’ and ‘indirect’ describe whether it can be traced to a product. A supervisor’s salary is fixed and indirect; a piece-rate worker’s wages are variable and direct. A cost can be any combination.

Where it breaks. No cost is fixed for ever. Rent is fixed within a range of output, but a larger plant needs more space. The same holds for the ‘relevant range’ in every textbook: a cost is only fixed or variable within it.

For exams. Give the definition and one example of each type, and state the formula for prime cost and total cost.

Fixed is stuck, variable follows; direct is traced, indirect is shared.

Go deeper for practitioners

Step costs. Some costs are fixed in steps: one supervisor can manage 20 workers, so a 21st needs a second. Treating this as a smooth line misleads the break-even analysis in the next chapter, which assumes costs behave simply.

A decision. A call centre pays a fixed ₹3 lakh a month for the premises and ₹40 a call for a telecom plan. Sort each cost, then say what happens to the cost per call as calls double.

blocks.title: Preparing a cost sheet
blocks.html:
Madurai Handlooms made 4,000 pieces last year. The owner asks: what did each piece cost, and what price gives a 20% profit? A cost sheet builds the answer step by step.

In plain wordsA cost sheet adds up the costs in stages, starting with materials and ending with the selling price, so you can see the cost at each stage.

Exam definitionA cost sheet is a statement showing the detailed cost elements for a product or period. It determines the total cost, the cost per unit and the selling price: Prime cost, Factory cost, Cost of production, Cost of sales and Selling price.

ParticularsAmountPer piece
Opening stock of material ₹50,000 + Purchases ₹4,50,000 − Closing stock ₹80,000₹4,20,000₹105
Add: Direct labour₹2,00,000₹50
Add: Direct expenses₹30,000₹8
Prime cost₹6,50,000₹162
Add: Factory overheads₹1,30,000₹32
Factory cost₹7,80,000₹195
Add: Administrative overheads₹60,000₹15
Cost of production₹8,40,000₹210
Add: Selling and distribution overheads₹40,000₹10
Total cost (cost of sales)₹8,80,000₹220
Add: Profit at 20% of cost₹1,76,000₹44
Selling price₹10,56,000₹264

The sheet assumes all pieces made were sold and no work was left in progress. Where there is unfinished work or stock of finished goods, the opening and closing balances of each are adjusted at the matching stage.

Prime cost → + Factory OH → Factory cost → + Admin OH → Cost of production → + Selling OH → Total cost → + Profit → Selling price

Don’t mix up profit on cost and profit on sales. A 20% profit on cost of ₹8,80,000 is ₹1,76,000. As a share of the selling price of ₹10,56,000 it is only 16.7%. Always check which base the question uses.

Where it breaks. Overheads are allocated by a rule (such as per labour hour), so the cost per piece depends on the rule. The sheet is also a statement of the past. It is a guide to price, not a promise that the market will pay it.

For exams. Follow the order of the stages, show each sub-total, and watch the opening and closing stocks and the profit base.

Prime, factory, production, sales, price: each stage adds its own overhead.

Go deeper for practitioners

Overheads in the middle. Notice that the factory overhead of ₹1,30,000 is added to prime cost, the administrative overhead to the factory cost, and so on. Stock of finished goods is valued at the cost of production, not at the total cost, because selling costs are not incurred until the piece is sold.

A decision. A rival will sell similar pieces at ₹250. Madurai’s total cost is ₹220 a piece. What could it cut, and what would it give up if it matched the price?

chapters.title: Activity-Based and Life-Cycle Costing
chapters.scope: How ABC charges overhead by the activities that cause it, and how life-cycle costing counts the whole cost of a product or an asset.

blocks.title: Activity-based costing: the ideas
blocks.html:
A factory makes a standard gear in thousands and a custom gear in hundreds. Each month it sets up machines, inspects parts and orders material far more often for the custom gear. If overhead is shared by machine hours alone, the custom gear looks cheaper than it is.

In plain wordsActivity-based costing (ABC) charges overhead to products according to the activities each product causes, not just its volume. Costs are first traced to activities, then to products.

Exam definitionActivity-based costing is a system in which costs are first traced to activities and then to products, on the assumption that activities cause costs. Costs are charged to products according to each product’s use of each activity.

TermMeaningExample
Cost objectAnything for which a separate cost is wantedA product, service, project, customer or brand
Cost unitA unit of product, service or time for which cost is statedKilowatt-hour for a power firm
ActivityA group of tasks tied to a cost objectScheduling, set-ups, purchasing, inspecting
Cost poolA group of indirect costs with similar behaviour, one for each activityAll set-up costs together
Cost driverThe factor that causes the cost of an activityNumber of set-ups, kilometres run
Cost driver rateCost of the pool ÷ number of driver units₹6,000 a set-up

Three kinds of driver. A transaction driver counts how many times an activity is done (orders, inspections, set-ups). A duration driver counts the time it takes (set-up hours, inspection hours). An intensity driver charges directly for the resources used each time, for example a special inspection that uses an expensive tester.

BasisTraditional costingActivity-based costing
Cost flowsResources → departments → productsResources → activities → products
Base for overheadUsually volume: labour or machine hoursMany drivers, one for each activity
Cause and effectWeakDirect, by activity
Best suited toFew products, low overheadMany products, and overhead a large share of cost

Don’t confuse a cost pool with a cost driver. The pool is the money: all the set-up costs added together. The driver is the cause you divide it by: the number of set-ups. The pool divided by the driver units gives the rate.

Where it breaks. ABC needs good data and takes effort to set up, and the choice of activities and drivers is a judgement. Facility-level costs, such as the factory building, have no real driver, and any rule for sharing them is arbitrary. A firm with one product gains little.

For exams. Know the six terms, the three kinds of driver, the features of ABC and the comparison with traditional costing.

Activities cause costs; products use activities.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why overhead has grown. In a firm of the past, labour was most of the cost, so labour hours were a fair base. In a modern plant, machines, planning, quality checks and design are a large part of cost, and they do not rise with labour hours. That is why ABC became useful as overhead became a bigger share of cost.

A decision. A bank branch charges every customer the same overhead per account. Which customers would ABC show to be costing more than they pay, and what could the bank do about it?

blocks.title: The steps of ABC and a worked example
blocks.html:
Hosur Gears makes 8,000 standard gears and 1,000 custom gears with ₹6,00,000 of overhead. Charged by labour hours, the custom gear carries ₹120 of overhead. What does it actually cost to make?

In plain wordsABC works in four steps: identify the activities, put their costs in pools, choose a driver for each pool, and charge each product for what it uses.

Exam definitionThe steps in an ABC system are: identifying activities; assigning costs to activity cost centres (cost pools); selecting appropriate cost drivers; and assigning the cost of the activities to products according to each product’s demand for the activities.

Four levels of activity (Cooper and Kaplan). Unit-level activities occur with every unit made (machining, testing each item). Batch-level activities occur once per batch (ordering, set-ups, inspecting a lot). Product-level activities support a product line (design, drawings, product advertising). Facility-level activities support the whole plant (building upkeep, security, the plant manager’s salary). ABC matters most when batch and product-level costs are a big share of the total.

Standard gearCustom gearTotal
Units made8,0001,0009,000
Direct labour hours8,0002,00010,000
Batches (set-ups)103040
Inspections206080
Activity poolCostDriverDriver unitsRate
Set-ups₹2,40,000Batches40₹6,000 a batch
Inspection₹80,000Inspections80₹1,000 each
General factory₹2,80,000Labour hours10,000₹28 an hour
Total₹6,00,000
Standard gearCustom gear
Set-ups₹60,000₹1,80,000
Inspection₹20,000₹60,000
General factory₹2,24,000₹56,000
ABC overhead₹3,04,000₹2,96,000
ABC overhead per unit₹38₹296
Traditional overhead at ₹60 a labour hour₹4,80,000₹1,20,000
Traditional overhead per unit₹60₹120

Traditional costing gives the custom gear ₹120 of overhead a unit, and ABC gives it ₹296. The standard gear is the other way round: ₹60 against ₹38. If the custom gear sells for ₹300 and has ₹100 of direct cost, traditional costing shows a profit of ₹80 a unit and ABC shows a loss of ₹96. The standard gear has been paying for part of the custom gear’s complexity.

Don’t think ABC creates cost. The total overhead, ₹6,00,000, is the same under both methods: ₹4,80,000 + ₹1,20,000 against ₹3,04,000 + ₹2,96,000. ABC only shares it differently, by cause. Only the split between products changes.

Where it breaks. The result depends on the pools and drivers chosen. Too few pools return to the traditional answer, and too many cost more to run than they are worth. Unit-level and facility-level costs are still shared on volume. A price rise alone may not be the right response to a loss on a product; redesign or fewer set-ups may be better.

For exams. Show the pools, the driver rates, the charge to each product and the comparison with the traditional method.

Pool the cost, find the driver, charge by use.

Go deeper for practitioners

What management can do. The ABC figures point to actions: cut the number of set-ups by making longer runs, simplify the custom gear, or price it to cover its true cost. Many firms use ABC for pricing, product-mix and cost-reduction choices rather than for the formal accounts.

A decision. Hosur’s customers for the custom gear say they will leave if the price rises to ₹420. Using ABC, what would you propose to keep them and stay profitable?

blocks.title: Life-cycle costing
blocks.html:
A hospital can buy a scanner for ₹70 lakh or for ₹1 crore. The cheaper one costs more to run and repair. Which is better? The purchase price is only one part of what an asset costs over its whole life.

In plain wordsLife-cycle costing adds every cost of a product or an asset from its first idea to its disposal, so choices are judged on the whole life and not just the price on the day.

Exam definitionLife-cycle costing is a system that tracks and accumulates the actual costs and revenues attributable to a cost object from its invention to its abandonment. Life cycle cost is the total cost of ownership: the cost to acquire, operate, support and finally dispose of an item, usually discounted to a common basis.

Product life-cycle costingProject (whole-life) costing
ConcernsA product or service in the marketA physical asset or project
Starts atIdentifying a customer needFeasibility study and acquisition
IncludesResearch, design, development, tooling, making, selling, distribution, product support, withdrawalPurchase, transport, installation, running, energy, maintenance, training, spare parts, retirement and disposal
Used toSee the long-term profit of a product against the early costs of design and launchChoose between assets and plan budgets

Stages of a product’s life. Market research, specification, design, prototype, development, tooling, manufacture, selling, distribution, product support, and decommissioning. Much of the cost is fixed in design, long before production begins.

Characteristics. It traces costs and revenues over several periods. It compares design and development costs with the revenue of the product. Each phase brings its own threats and opportunities. The life of a product can sometimes be extended by finding new users or new uses.

Choosing a machine. Machine X costs ₹10,00,000 and runs and is maintained for ₹1,50,000 a year. Machine Y costs ₹7,00,000 and costs ₹2,50,000 a year to run. Each lasts 5 years and then sells for ₹1,00,000 (X) or ₹50,000 (Y). The firm discounts at 10%, with running costs at each year-end.

Machine XMachine Y
Purchase price₹10,00,000₹7,00,000
Running costs over 5 years (undiscounted)₹7,50,000₹12,50,000
Less: sale at the end−₹1,00,000−₹50,000
Life-cycle cost, undiscounted₹16,50,000₹19,00,000
Life-cycle cost, discounted at 10%₹15,06,526₹16,16,651

Machine Y is ₹3,00,000 cheaper to buy, but over its life it costs about ₹1,10,125 more in present-value terms. The discounted figures use an annuity factor of 3.7908 for the running costs and 0.6209 for the sale in year 5.

Don’t decide on purchase price alone. Using the price alone overstates the return on the cheaper asset and understates the budget needed to run it. A budget that leaves out future running costs makes profit look larger than it will be.

Where it breaks. Future costs, lives and sale values are estimates, and the answer can flip if the discount rate or life changes. Benefits are not always the same for each choice, so cost alone may not be the test. Costs such as downtime or disposal rules are easy to overlook.

For exams. Know the two types, the stages of a product’s life, the heads of whole-life cost, and the three purposes: choose between assets, judge benefits and build accurate budgets.

Count the cost of owning, not just the cost of buying.

Go deeper for practitioners

Design decides cost. The largest part of a product’s lifetime cost is usually committed at the design stage, even though most of it is spent later. That is why life-cycle costing pushes cost thinking back into design and specification, where changes are cheap.

A decision. A municipality can buy a ₹20 lakh diesel bus or a ₹30 lakh electric bus. List the life-cycle cost heads you would estimate for each, and say which estimate you trust least.

chapters.title: Target Costing, Kaizen Costing and Just-in-Time
chapters.scope: Three Japanese-inspired ways to manage cost: set cost from the market price, cut it a little every month, and remove the waste of stock.

blocks.title: Target costing
blocks.html:
Chennai Mixers has designed a mixer-grinder that costs ₹2,650 to make. Rivals sell similar ones for ₹3,000. Adding its usual 20% to cost gives ₹3,180, which no buyer will pay. Is the answer to lower the margin, or to lower the cost?

In plain wordsTarget costing starts from the price the market will pay, takes away the profit the firm wants, and treats what is left as the most the product may cost. The task is then to design the product to that cost.

Exam definitionTarget cost is a cost estimate derived by subtracting a desired profit margin from a competitive market price. Target costing is a management technique in which prices are set by market conditions and costs are planned and managed out of a product early, in design and development.

Target cost = Selling price − Desired profit

The mixer-grinder. Market price ₹3,000. Desired profit 20% of price = ₹600. Target cost = ₹3,000 − ₹600 = ₹2,400. The first design costs ₹2,650, so there is a gap of ₹250 to be designed out.

ActionSaving per unit
Redesign the casing and remove a part₹120
Renegotiate the motor price with the supplier₹80
Cut a step from assembly₹50
Total₹250

If the design could not be changed and the firm sold at ₹3,000, it would earn ₹350, which is only 11.7% of the price against the 20% wanted.

Why use it. When products are alike, competition is strong and customers switch easily, the firm cannot set the price, so it must control the cost. Most of a product’s cost is fixed at the design stage, so the saving must be sought there, not after production has begun.

StepWhat happens
1. Market researchLearn what customers want and what they will pay
2. Maximum costSet the profit margin and from it the highest allowable cost
3. Design the productEngineers and designers create it to that cost
4. Analysis and adjustmentCompare design cost with the target; redesign or cut costs if over
5. Design improvement and trialsTest features; continue until cost and customer needs are both met
6. Management approvalPresent the design, tests and cost to management
7. Record keepingKeep accounts to check costs stay within the target
8. ImplementationMake the product, and keep checking cost and quality

Objectives. To lower the cost of new products so that the required profit is ensured; to meet the quality, delivery time and price the market needs; and to make everyone in the firm responsible for the target profit.

Benefits. Better profit through lower cost, innovation shaped by what customers want, customer satisfaction, and a leaner production process.

Don’t confuse target costing with cost-plus pricing. Cost-plus starts with cost and adds profit to reach a price. Target costing starts with the price and takes profit away to reach a cost. The first lets inefficiency pass into the price; the second makes the cost bear the pressure of the market.

Where it breaks. A target set too hard may lead designers to cut quality or safety, or to push the cost onto suppliers who cannot bear it. A product with no real market price, such as a new invention, has nothing to start from. The work in design and testing adds cost of its own.

For exams. Know the formula, the contrast with cost-plus, the objectives, the steps and the benefits.

Price first, profit second, cost is what is left.

Go deeper for practitioners

Value engineering. The main tool for closing the gap is to study each part of the product for what it does for the customer and what it costs, then to remove features the customer does not value or to find a cheaper way to deliver the ones they do. Cost is taken out in design, not squeezed in the factory.

A decision. A target cost calls for dropping a feature that your sales team says some customers like. How would you decide whether to keep it?

blocks.title: Kaizen costing
blocks.html:
Chennai Mixers launches at the target cost of ₹2,400. A year later rivals have cut theirs. If cost stays still, the margin shrinks. Kaizen costing keeps cost falling by a little each month.

In plain wordsKaizen is the Japanese word for continuous improvement. Kaizen costing sets a small cost-reduction target each period for products already being made, and everyone looks for waste to remove.

Exam definitionKaizen costing is a system for continuing cost reduction of existing products and processes. Targets for cost reduction are set regularly, for example monthly, and variance analysis at the end of each period compares the target reduction with the actual. It focuses on cost reduction rather than cost control.

The mixer-grinder, month by month. The unit cost is ₹2,400. The target is to take ₹20 off every month.

MonthTarget unit costActual unit costVariance
1₹2,380₹2,385₹5 A
2₹2,360₹2,355₹5 F
3₹2,340₹2,345₹5 A
4₹2,320₹2,310₹10 F

In months 1 and 3 the firm fell short of its target and in months 2 and 4 it beat it. After four months the actual cost is ₹2,310, which is ₹90 below the start. The variance is a prompt to find which waste was removed, and which was not.

Continuous improvement, not re-engineering. Kaizen is small steps taken all the time by everyone. Business process re-engineering is a radical, one-off change. The thinking behind Kaizen is that perfection is never reached, so there is always something to improve, and that improvements from the people who do the work are usually small.

WasteWhat it means
Over-productionMaking more than customers have ordered
InventoryHolding or buying stock that is not needed
WaitingDelays and idle time that add no value
DefectsParts that are scrapped or must be reworked
MotionMovements of people or machines that add no value
TransportationMoving material or work-in-progress more than needed, because of poor layout
Over-processingSteps that add no value for the customer

Principles. It does not take the present situation as given. It seeks gradual improvements, not perfection at any cost. It allows managers to use their knowledge and discretion and encourages shared decision-making, on the view that many minds do better than one. Standards are set and then improved continually.

Don’t treat Kaizen as the same as standard costing. A standard cost is a fixed yardstick, and a variance is judged against it. In Kaizen costing the yardstick itself is lowered every period. Kaizen costing is about reducing the cost, while standard costing is about controlling it at the level set.

Where it breaks. Targets that keep falling can run out of room, and employees may feel pressure when no improvement is ever enough. Gains from small steps need a culture that rewards suggestions. Cutting cost without regard to quality can harm customers.

For exams. Give the meaning, the contrast with cost control and with re-engineering, the seven wastes and the principles.

Small cuts, every month, by everyone.

Go deeper for practitioners

Target costing and Kaizen together. Target costing fixes the cost at launch, through design. Kaizen costing then takes over for the life of the product, taking cost down in steps. Together they cover the whole life: design to the market price, then improve.

A decision. A supervisor reports she has met every Kaizen target for a year, but quality complaints have risen. What would you check, and what would you change about the targets?

blocks.title: Just-in-time (JIT)
blocks.html:
Chennai Mixers holds about ₹12,00,000 of motors, castings and finished goods. At 20% a year for storage, insurance, interest and spoilage, holding it costs ₹2,40,000 a year. What if the goods arrived only when they were needed?

In plain wordsJust-in-time brings materials and parts exactly when the factory needs them, and makes goods only as customers order them. The idea is that stock is waste.

Exam definitionJust-in-time (JIT) is an inventory management method in which labour, materials and goods are re-filled or scheduled to arrive exactly when needed in the manufacturing process. Its philosophy is that inventory is waste. It stands for producing the required units, in the required quantities, at the required time.

The saving. Suppose JIT cuts the average stock from ₹12,00,000 to ₹3,00,000. Carrying cost falls from ₹2,40,000 to ₹60,000, a saving of ₹1,80,000 a year, and ₹9,00,000 of working capital is freed.

Where it came from. JIT was developed at Toyota, and Taiichi Ohno is usually called its father. It worked only because everyone was committed, the plant was laid out for efficient flow, and quality and production schedules matched demand.

Objective
Minimise the cost of production
Link suppliers with the manufacturer and save material and time
Improve processes and systems continuously
Reduce the cost of products and meet customer needs
Raise efficiency and cut waste in materials, time and effort
Reach the best balance of quality and cost
EnvironmentWhat it means
ProductionBuy, make, assemble and deliver each stage just in time for the next: ideally one unit in process and no finished stock
InventoryBuy materials just in time; make or assemble to order
ServicesSchedule trained service staff and tasks to fit the orders, ‘service to order’
InformationKeep the necessary information ready and up to date, linked with those who need it

JIT purchasing in steps. Find a reliable supplier. Work out the internal and external lead times. Prepare the bill of materials and the master production schedule against time. Order the items to arrive within the lead times. Move material straight to the shop floor, make or assemble to schedule, and deliver as planned. A small temporary store may be kept if needed. The aim is to remove the warehouse and its carrying cost.

Don’t think JIT only means less stock. JIT needs steady quality, short set-ups, reliable suppliers and a tight schedule. A firm that cuts stock without these simply runs out of parts. The stock was hiding problems, and JIT exposes them, so they must be solved.

Where it breaks. A supply failure stops the line at once, because there is no buffer. Heavy dependence on a few suppliers, long supply routes or sudden demand swings make JIT risky. Some firms now hold a safety stock of critical parts.

For exams. Know the meaning, the slogan ‘inventory is waste’, the origin, the objectives, the four environments and the steps of JIT purchasing.

The right unit, in the right quantity, at the right time.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why the three belong together. Target costing sets the cost at design. Kaizen costing reduces it continuously. JIT removes the waste of stock and waiting. All three treat waste as the enemy, and cost reduction as everyone’s job.

A decision. A firm wants to adopt JIT, but its main supplier is 600 km away and has twice been late. What would you do before cutting stock?

chapters.title: Marginal Costing and Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis
chapters.scope: Contribution, the break-even point and margin of safety, and how marginal costing guides short-term decisions.

blocks.title: Marginal costing and contribution
blocks.html:
A pump-maker’s costs are mostly the factory itself. Its materials and wages are only a part. Should the factory’s rent be charged to each pump? The answer changes the profit, and the decision.

In plain wordsMarginal costing counts only the costs that rise with each extra unit. Fixed costs are charged to the period, not to the product. What each unit earns above its variable cost is its contribution.

Exam definitionMarginal costing considers only variable costs as product costs; fixed costs are treated as period costs. Contribution is sales minus variable cost, and profit is contribution minus fixed costs.

One product. Coimbatore Pumps sells a pump at ₹50. Each pump costs ₹30 in variable cost, and fixed costs are ₹1,20,000 a year.

ConceptFormulaPumps
ContributionSales − Variable cost₹1,60,000 on 8,000 pumps
Contribution per unitSelling price − Variable cost per unit₹50 − ₹30 = ₹20
P/V ratio(Contribution ÷ Sales) × 10040%
ProfitContribution − Fixed costs₹1,60,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹40,000

Marginal against absorption costing. The factory makes 10,000 pumps and sells 8,000, leaving 2,000 in stock. Absorption costing spreads the fixed cost over all made, ₹12 a pump, so a pump is valued at ₹42. Marginal costing values it at ₹30.

Marginal costingAbsorption costing
Value of closing stock of 2,000 pumps₹60,000₹84,000
Profit₹40,000₹64,000
Difference₹24,000 = 2,000 pumps × ₹12 of fixed cost carried forward

The absorption profit is higher because ₹24,000 of this year’s fixed cost is carried forward in stock to a later year. Over a firm’s life, both methods report the same total profit.

Don’t call contribution profit. Contribution is what is left of sales after variable costs, and is meant to cover fixed costs first. Only the part above fixed costs is profit. Below the break-even point the contribution exists, yet the firm makes a loss.

Where it breaks. Marginal costing is meant for short-term decisions. Over the long run all costs, including the fixed ones, must be recovered by price. Accounting standards for published accounts require stock to be valued at full (absorption) cost, so marginal costing is a management tool, not the basis of the statutory accounts.

For exams. Know the formulas, the difference in stock valuation, and the reason why marginal and absorption profits differ.

Variable costs go in the product; fixed costs wait in the period.

Go deeper for practitioners

Production against sales. If production equals sales, both methods give the same profit. If production exceeds sales, absorption profit is higher. If sales exceed production, it is lower. This is why a manager measured on absorption profit may be tempted to build stock at year-end.

A decision. A manager’s bonus depends on reported profit under absorption costing. What could she do in March to raise it without selling anything more, and how would marginal costing remove the temptation?

blocks.title: Marginal cost, its features and limits
blocks.html:
A printer makes 100 articles for ₹50,000 and 101 for ₹50,450. The 101st article added ₹450 to the bill. That ₹450 is what marginal costing is built on.

In plain wordsMarginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit, which is its variable cost. Marginal costing studies how profit changes when volume or type of output changes, by splitting costs into fixed and variable.

Exam definitionMarginal cost is the amount by which aggregate cost changes if output is increased or decreased by one unit. Marginal costing is the ascertainment of marginal costs and of the effect on profit of changes in volume or type of output by differentiating between fixed and variable costs. It is also called variable costing, contributory costing and comparative costing.

Why only variable cost. Within the existing capacity, one more unit raises only variable cost. Fixed costs stay as they are. So the cost of the extra unit is its variable cost, and fixed costs are charged to the period against the contribution.

FeatureMeaning
Only variable costs go in the productFixed costs are recovered from contribution
All costs split into fixed and variableSemi-variable costs are divided into the two parts
Closing stock at variable cost onlyNo fixed overhead is carried forward in stock
CVP and break-even analysis are part of itThey follow from the contribution idea

Several products, one fixed cost. A firm sells three products and has fixed costs of ₹80,000.

ABCTotal
Units10,00020,00060,00090,000
Selling price per unit₹10₹10₹5
Variable cost per unit₹6₹7.50₹4.50
Contribution per unit₹4₹2.50₹0.50
Contribution₹40,000₹50,000₹30,000₹1,20,000
Less: Fixed costs−₹80,000
Profit₹40,000

Each product adds to the pool that pays the fixed costs. Product C has the thinnest margin per unit, ₹0.50, but its volume makes it worth ₹30,000.

AdvantagesLimitations
Useful data for decisionsSplitting semi-variable costs into fixed and variable parts is hard in practice
A good tool for profit planningLeaving out fixed costs in decisions can lead to wrong conclusions
No arbitrary sharing of fixed costsIt ignores fixed costs that rise with new technology
Avoids the problem of a fixed overhead rateIt does not suit cost-plus contracts
Leads to break-even and CVP analysisStock valued at variable cost does not match published accounts

Don’t mix up marginal cost with the average cost of a unit. Average cost spreads fixed costs over all units, and falls as output rises. Marginal cost is only the extra cost of one more, and is constant when variable cost per unit is. A firm that prices on average cost can turn down an order that would have added profit.

Where it breaks. The method assumes variable costs per unit are constant and that there is spare capacity. Near full capacity, the next unit may need new plant, and its cost is far higher than the variable cost. Published accounts must value stock at full cost, so marginal costing is only for internal use.

For exams. Know the definitions and the three alternative names, the features, and the advantages and limitations, and be ready to prepare a statement for more than one product.

Extra unit, extra variable cost; fixed cost waits for the contribution.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why the 101st unit matters. Marginal cost is a rule for the next decision: should we make one more, or take one more order? It does not tell us whether the whole business pays. For that, contribution must exceed fixed costs.

A decision. A firm’s product C has a contribution of only ₹0.50 a unit. Should it drop C to save effort? What would happen to profit if it did?

blocks.title: Break-even and cost-volume-profit analysis
blocks.html:
Before opening a second shop, a trader asks: how many sales do I need just to cover my costs? Cost-volume-profit analysis answers that, and tells how a rise or fall in sales moves the profit.

In plain wordsThe break-even point is the sale at which there is no profit and no loss. Above it, each extra unit adds its contribution to profit.

Exam definitionCost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis studies the relationship between cost, volume and profit. At the break-even point, contribution equals fixed costs. The margin of safety is actual sales minus break-even sales.

ConceptFormulaResult
Break-even (units)Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹20 = 6,000 pumps
Break-even (₹)Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio₹1,20,000 ÷ 0.4 = ₹3,00,000
Margin of safetyActual sales − Break-even sales₹4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000 = ₹1,00,000 (25% of sales)
Target profit (units)(Fixed cost + Desired profit) ÷ Contribution per unit(₹1,20,000 + ₹1,00,000) ÷ ₹20 = 11,000 pumps
Target profit (₹)(Fixed cost + Desired profit) ÷ P/V ratio₹2,20,000 ÷ 0.4 = ₹5,50,000

At 8,000 pumps, sales are ₹4,00,000 and the margin of safety is ₹1,00,000, or 2,000 pumps. Sales could fall by 25% before the firm made a loss.

The assumptions. Selling price and variable cost per unit stay constant. Fixed costs stay constant within the range considered. All production is sold, with no closing stock. The product mix does not change.

Don’t use the unit formula when the question gives sales in rupees. Both formulas give the same result: ₹3,00,000 is 6,000 pumps at ₹50. The P/V ratio form works in rupees, which is useful when a firm sells many products at different prices.

Where it breaks. Real costs are not straight lines. A price cut to win volume changes the contribution. Fixed costs rise in steps. Competition and inflation move prices and costs. The analysis is a simplification, best for short-term what-if questions and less suited to long-term planning.

For exams. Write the formulas in both units and rupees, and state the assumptions and limitations.

Break-even is where contribution equals fixed cost.

Go deeper for practitioners

Operating leverage. A firm with high fixed costs and low variable costs has a large contribution per unit. Its profit rises sharply once above break-even, and falls just as sharply below it. That is why a small drop in sales hurts such a firm, and why the margin of safety matters.

A decision. The pump-maker is offered a machine that cuts variable cost to ₹25 but adds ₹30,000 to fixed costs. Calculate the new break-even point and say at what volume the machine pays for itself.

blocks.title: Relationships in CVP and the angle of incidence
blocks.html:
At the break-even point, sales are ₹3,00,000. At sales of ₹4,00,000, profit is ₹40,000. How are these linked? A handful of identities answer almost every CVP question.

In plain wordsIn CVP analysis, contribution pays the fixed cost first and then becomes profit. At break-even, all of it goes to fixed cost. Above break-even, every rupee of contribution is profit.

Exam definitionThe marginal cost equation is S − V = F + P. At the break-even point, C = F. At the margin of safety, C = P. The P/V ratio is the contribution as a percentage of sales, and also the change in profit as a percentage of the change in sales.

IdeaFormulaPumps
Marginal cost equationSales − Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit₹4,00,000 − ₹2,40,000 = ₹1,20,000 + ₹40,000
At break-evenContribution = Fixed cost₹1,20,000 = ₹1,20,000
In the margin of safetyContribution = Profit₹40,000 = ₹40,000
Margin of safetyProfit ÷ P/V ratio₹40,000 ÷ 0.40 = ₹1,00,000
P/V ratio from two yearsChange in profit ÷ Change in sales₹16,000 ÷ ₹40,000 = 40%

Required sales for a target profit. In units: (Fixed cost + Desired profit) ÷ Contribution per unit. In rupees: (Fixed cost + Desired profit) ÷ P/V ratio. (Some books swap the two; the units formula divides by contribution per unit, and the rupees formula by the ratio.)

The angle of incidence. It is the angle at which the sales line cuts the total cost line at break-even on the chart. A wide angle means that profit grows fast once sales pass break-even, a sign of high earning power. A narrow angle means that profit builds slowly.

CVP against break-even analysis. CVP analysis studies how profit responds to changes in cost and volume. Break-even analysis finds the level of activity at which sales equal total cost, and the profit at other levels. The two are so closely linked that the terms are often used for each other.

What CVP is used for. To forecast profit, to plan it, to find the break-even point, to build flexible budgets, and to judge performance against plan.

Don’t assume the margin of safety is a profit. The margin of safety is a sales figure. Only the contribution on it, the profit, is money. In the example, the margin of safety is ₹1,00,000 of sales, and the profit is ₹40,000, which is 40% of that.

Where it breaks. The identities hold only while selling price, variable cost per unit and fixed costs stay constant. A firm with a mix of products needs the average P/V ratio, which changes if the mix changes.

For exams. Memorise the identities, the P/V ratio from two periods, and the meaning of a wide angle of incidence.

Break-even: contribution equals fixed cost. Above it: contribution equals profit.

Go deeper for practitioners

Mix changes the answer. If a firm sells two products with different P/V ratios, selling more of the richer one moves break-even down, even though total sales do not change. This is why a sales manager and a finance manager may disagree on which sales to push.

A decision. A firm’s sales rose from ₹3,60,000 to ₹4,00,000 and profit from ₹24,000 to ₹40,000. Find its P/V ratio, then its fixed cost, and its break-even sales.

blocks.title: Using marginal costing for decisions
blocks.html:
A buyer abroad offers ₹40 a pump for 1,000 pumps, below the usual ₹50. The cost sheet says a pump costs ₹42. Should the firm refuse? Marginal costing says to look at what changes.

In plain wordsIn a short-term decision only the costs and revenues that change with the choice matter. Fixed costs that continue either way are left out.

Exam definitionMarginal costing supports pricing, make-or-buy, export orders, shutdown decisions and profit planning by comparing the extra revenue of a choice with the extra variable cost it causes.

DecisionFull-cost viewMarginal view
Export order of 1,000 pumps at ₹40, using spare capacity₹40 is below the cost of ₹42, so refuseEach pump adds ₹10 of contribution: ₹10,000. Accept.
Buy a component at ₹38 instead of making it (full cost ₹42, variable cost ₹30, fixed cost continues)₹38 is below ₹42, so buyMaking costs ₹30 of extra cost; buying costs ₹38. Buying adds ₹8 a unit. Make it.
Close a product line that does not cover its full costA loss, so close itIf it still covers its variable cost, it adds to the fixed costs. Keep it until something better uses the capacity.

In each case the fixed costs are the same whichever way the firm decides, so they should not tip the choice.

Don’t forget the limits that make the marginal view safe. The export order must use idle capacity, must not be sold in the home market at the lower price, and must not lead other customers to demand a discount. If the order displaces a full-price sale, the lost contribution is a cost of accepting it.

Where it breaks. A firm that prices every order at marginal cost never recovers its fixed costs, and will fail. The method suits the occasional, special case. The usual price must cover total cost and profit.

For exams. Use the marginal view for each decision, state its assumption of spare capacity, and say that fixed costs are ignored only because they do not change.

Ask what changes. Ignore what stays.

Go deeper for practitioners

Opportunity cost. If the factory is already full, an export order uses capacity that would otherwise make full-price pumps. The relevant cost is then the variable cost plus the contribution given up, which can exceed the offer.

A decision. A hotel has empty rooms in the monsoon, with variable cost of ₹600 per room-night. A travel agent offers ₹1,500 a night for 50 rooms. List what you would check before accepting, and what you would do if the agent resold the rooms on a booking site at ₹3,000.

chapters.title: Standard Costing and Variance Analysis
chapters.scope: How standard costs are used as a yardstick, and how material, labour and overhead variances show where actual cost departed from it.

blocks.title: Standard costing and variances
blocks.html:
The standard cost of the 900 utensils Salem Steel Utensils made was ₹5,58,000. It actually spent ₹6,04,850. That is ₹46,850 over. A manager needs to know where the money went, not only that it went.

In plain wordsStandard costing sets what a unit should cost under good working conditions, then compares it with what it did cost. Each gap is a variance, and each variance points to a cause to look into.

Exam definitionStandard costing is a control technique that compares predetermined (standard) costs with actual costs to identify variances, analyse their causes and take corrective action. Variance = Standard cost − Actual cost; favourable (F) when standard exceeds actual, adverse (A) when standard is less than actual.

ElementQuantityRateStandard cost
Material4 kg₹50₹200
Labour3 hours₹80₹240
Variable overhead3 hours₹20₹60
Fixed overhead3 hours₹40 (₹1,20,000 ÷ 3,000 hours)₹120
Standard cost₹620

The steps. Set the standard, measure the actual cost, compare the two, identify the variances and their causes, and report and act on them.

The sign. This chapter follows the usual rule: a variance is favourable when the actual cost is less than the standard, and adverse when it is more. In the tables that follow, F means a gain and A a loss.

MCV = MPV + MUV | LCV = LRV + LEV + LITV | VOCV = VOEV + VOEEV | FOCV = FOEV + FOVV

Don’t compare actual cost with the budget for a different output. Salem’s standards are set for one utensil. The standard cost of the 900 actually made is the yardstick, not the cost of the 1,000 budgeted. Comparing with the budgeted output mixes a volume effect into every variance.

Where it breaks. Standards are estimates, and can be set too loose (easy to beat) or too tight (always missed). If prices are rising fast, the standards go out of date. A variance is a question, not a verdict: an adverse usage variance may come from poor material, not poor work.

For exams. Know the order of the steps, the sign convention, and the four total-variance identities.

Set, measure, compare, find the cause, act.

Go deeper for practitioners

Who owns a variance? A price variance on material is usually the buyer’s, a usage variance the production manager’s, a rate variance the HR or union agreement, and an efficiency variance the supervisor’s. Assigning each to an owner is what makes the system a control, not just a calculation.

A decision. A purchasing manager buys cheaper steel and the material price variance is favourable. The production manager complains of an adverse usage variance. How would you decide whether the saving was real?

blocks.title: Standards, and the case for standard costing
blocks.html:
A cement plant makes the same product all year. If each month’s cost differs a little, is that bad luck or poor control? Only a yardstick set in advance can tell.

In plain wordsA standard cost is what a unit ought to cost under stated working conditions. It differs from an estimate, which is a guess at what it will cost.

Exam definitionStandard cost is a predetermined cost based on a technical estimate for materials, labour and overhead for a selected period and a prescribed set of working conditions. Standard costing is the preparation and use of standard costs, their comparison with actual costs, and the analysis of variances to their causes and points of incidence.

Standard costEstimated cost
What the cost should beWhat the cost will be
Set by technical experts, allowing for efficiencyBased on past data, adjusted for trends
Measures efficiencyCannot measure efficiency
A tool of cost controlDoes not serve cost control
Part of the accounting processStatistical; may stay outside the accounts
Used where standard costing is in operationCan be used in any historical cost system
StandardWhat it assumesUse
IdealThe best conditions: no waste, no power cuts, no idle timeA target; rarely reached
BasicFixed in a base year and never changedLittle use in practice
CurrentPresent conditions, set for a short periodWidely used for control
ExpectedWhat is expected to be reached in the period aheadRelevant for business planning
NormalAverages of the past, carried forwardNot much relevance

Where it suits. Standard costing works best for firms making standard products again and again, such as cement, steel or sugar. It suits jobbing work poorly, because every job is different and a standard for each would cost too much to set.

Advantages. It gives management a way to judge performance. It helps in fixing standards and in production planning and pricing. It is a measuring rod for variances, and it helps remove inefficiency through corrective action.

Management by exception. A variance flags a result that is not as planned, whether better or worse. Management can spend its time on the large or repeated variances and leave results that follow the standard alone.

Don’t treat an ideal standard as a fair test. An ideal standard assumes no waste and no breakdowns. Workers can never reach it, so adverse variances will always appear and may be ignored. A current or expected standard, set at attainable levels, is more useful for control.

Where it breaks. Standards go out of date when prices or methods change, and then every variance is noise. They can also be too loose, which lets inefficiency pass. Setting and reviewing them costs time and money.

For exams. Know the definition, the difference from estimated cost, the five kinds of standard, the suitability and the advantages.

Standard: should be. Estimate: will be.

Go deeper for practitioners

Who sets the standard. Good standards come from engineers (quantities and times), purchasing (prices), and HR (wage rates), agreed with the managers who will be judged on them. Standards imposed from above tend to be resented and ignored.

A decision. A firm making tailor-made machines asks whether to adopt standard costing. What would you advise, and what part of the firm might still use standards?

blocks.title: Material and labour variances
blocks.html:
Salem used 3,800 kg of steel to make 900 utensils, against a standard of 3,600 kg, and paid ₹52 a kg instead of ₹50. Two causes, two variances, and each belongs to a different person.

In plain wordsA material or labour variance splits the extra cost into a price (or rate) part and a quantity (or time) part, so you can tell whether the firm paid too much or used too much.

Exam definitionMaterial cost variance = (SQ × SP) − (AQ × AP), made up of the price variance AQ × (SP − AP) and the usage variance SP × (SQ − AQ). Labour cost variance = (SH × SR) − (AH × AR), made up of the rate, efficiency and idle-time variances.

VarianceFormulaWorkingResult
Cost (MCV)(SQ × SP) − (AQ × AP)₹1,80,000 − ₹1,97,600₹17,600 A
Price (MPV)AQ × (SP − AP)3,800 × (₹50 − ₹52)₹7,600 A
Usage (MUV)SP × (SQ − AQ)₹50 × (3,600 − 3,800)₹10,000 A

SQ is the standard quantity for the actual output (900 × 4 kg = 3,600 kg). Price and usage add up to the cost variance.

Labour. Salem paid for 2,800 hours at ₹82, but 150 of them were idle (a power cut), so 2,650 hours were worked. The standard hours for 900 utensils are 2,700. Here AH in the cost and rate formulas means hours paid.

VarianceFormulaWorkingResult
Cost (LCV)(SH × SR) − (AH × AR)₹2,16,000 − ₹2,29,600₹13,600 A
Rate (LRV)AH × (SR − AR)2,800 × (₹80 − ₹82)₹5,600 A
Efficiency (LEV)SR × (SH − AH worked)₹80 × (2,700 − 2,650)₹4,000 F
Idle time (LITV)Idle hours × SR150 × ₹80₹12,000 A

Salem was ₹5,600 over on wage rate and ₹12,000 over on idle time, and gained ₹4,000 by working 50 hours faster than standard.

Mix and yield. When several materials are used, the usage variance splits further. A standard 100 kg input of A (60 kg at ₹10) and B (40 kg at ₹20) yields 80 kg. A batch used 700 kg of A and 300 kg of B and made 780 kg. Material usage variance is ₹650 F. The mix variance, SP × (RSQ − AQ), is ₹1,000 F, because the batch used more of the cheaper material. The yield variance is ₹350 A, as the output was 20 kg short of the 800 kg that 1,000 kg should give, at ₹17.50 a kg of output.

A second case to practise. Standard output was 800 units but 1,000 were made. Standard material was 1 kg a unit at ₹4, and 1,200 kg were used at ₹5. Cost variance = (1,000 × ₹4) − (1,200 × ₹5) = ₹2,000 A; price variance = 1,200 × (₹4 − ₹5) = ₹1,200 A; usage variance = ₹4 × (1,000 − 1,200) = ₹800 A. For labour, a standard rate of ₹3 an hour and 2 hours a unit, 160 units made, 300 hours worked at ₹3.5: standard hours are 320. Cost variance = ₹960 − ₹1,050 = ₹90 A; rate = 300 × (₹3 − ₹3.5) = ₹150 A; efficiency = ₹3 × (320 − 300) = ₹60 F.

Don’t treat idle time as efficiency. Idle time is paid time with no work, and is always adverse. The efficiency variance concerns the hours that were worked. Mixing the two hides a power cut inside a supervisor’s results.

Where it breaks. A favourable mix variance can come from using poorer material, which later shows as low yield. Read mix and yield together. A usage variance may also flow from poor purchases, so check the cause before blaming a person.

For exams. Write the formula first, then substitute. State SQ and SH as for actual output, and the sign convention.

Price for what you pay, usage for what you use; rate for the wage, efficiency for the hours.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why mix and yield add up to usage. Mix compares the actual input with the same total input in standard proportion. Yield compares the output the total input should give with the output actually obtained. Together, they account for all of the usage gap, which is why they total ₹650 favourable.

A decision. A dairy blends milk of two fat grades. The mix variance is favourable and the yield variance adverse. What may have happened in the plant, and what would you check?

blocks.title: Overhead variances
blocks.html:
Material and labour have a clear quantity and price. Overhead does not: factory rent and power are spread over many units. Variances show whether the firm spent more than it planned, or used the factory less than planned.

In plain wordsOverhead variances separate the extra spent from the extra or missed use of capacity. Variable overhead splits into expenditure and efficiency. Fixed overhead splits into expenditure and volume.

Exam definitionVariable overhead cost variance = (SH × SR) − (AH × AR), made up of expenditure and efficiency. Fixed overhead cost variance = Standard fixed overhead − Actual fixed overhead, made up of expenditure (Budgeted − Actual) and volume (Standard − Budgeted).

VarianceFormulaWorkingResult
Cost (VOCV)(SH × SR) − (AH × AR)₹54,000 − ₹55,650₹1,650 A
Expenditure (VOEV)AH × (SR − AR)2,650 × (₹20 − ₹21)₹2,650 A
Efficiency (VOEEV)SR × (SH − AH)₹20 × (2,700 − 2,650)₹1,000 F
VarianceFormulaWorkingResult
Cost (FOCV)Standard fixed OH − Actual fixed OH₹1,08,000 − ₹1,22,000₹14,000 A
Expenditure (FOEV)Budgeted fixed OH − Actual fixed OH₹1,20,000 − ₹1,22,000₹2,000 A
Volume (FOVV)Standard fixed OH − Budgeted fixed OH₹1,08,000 − ₹1,20,000₹12,000 A

Standard fixed overhead is the absorbed amount for the actual output: 2,700 hours × ₹40 = ₹1,08,000. Salem budgeted for 3,000 hours and worked fewer, so ₹12,000 of fixed overhead was not recovered by the output. That is the volume variance.

PartVariance
Material cost₹17,600 A
Labour cost₹13,600 A
Variable overhead₹1,650 A
Fixed overhead₹14,000 A
Total cost variance₹46,850 A (₹5,58,000 standard against ₹6,04,850 actual)

The overhead cost variance. The two parts together give the total overhead variance, recovered overhead less actual overhead. For Salem it is (₹54,000 + ₹1,08,000) − (₹55,650 + ₹1,22,000) = ₹15,650 A, which is ₹1,650 A for variable and ₹14,000 A for fixed. Typical causes: bills paid in advance or late, a breakdown that needed repairs, spoilage, overtime, or the same fixed spending spread over a different output.

Don’t call the volume variance a spending error. Salem did not overspend on fixed overhead by ₹12,000. The factory made fewer than budgeted, so the fixed cost was spread over fewer units. The cause is the sales or production plan, not the accounts payable desk.

Where it breaks. Fixed overhead is not controllable at the shop-floor level in the short run, so a volume variance mostly tests the plan. Variable overhead variances assume overhead follows hours, which is not true for all firms; activity-based costing uses other drivers.

For exams. Remember the pairs: expenditure and efficiency for variable; expenditure and volume for fixed. Learn each formula and say which part of the plant it tests.

Variable: spend and speed. Fixed: spend and volume.

Go deeper for practitioners

Using the total. Salem’s ₹46,850 shortfall is made up of ₹17,600 on steel, ₹13,600 on labour, ₹1,650 on variable overhead and ₹14,000 on fixed overhead. ₹34,000 of it (steel usage, idle time and the volume gap) comes from how the plant was run, not from prices. That is the kind of conclusion a variance report is meant to support.

A decision. A textile unit shows a large adverse fixed overhead volume variance for six months running. Is it a problem to fix, a standard to reset, or a plan to change?

blocks.title: Sales variances
blocks.html:
Salem budgeted to sell 1,000 utensils at ₹50. It sold 900 at ₹52. Revenue fell short by ₹3,200. Was it the price or the volume?

In plain wordsA sales variance compares actual sales with the budget and splits the gap into a price effect and a volume effect.

Exam definitionSales value variance is the difference between actual and budgeted sales. It is made up of the sales price variance, actual quantity × (Actual price − Standard price), and the sales volume variance, Standard price × (Actual quantity − Budgeted quantity). Favourable when actual sales exceed budget.

VarianceFormulaWorkingResult
ValueActual sales − Budgeted sales₹46,800 − ₹50,000₹3,200 A
PriceActual quantity × (Actual price − Standard price)900 × (₹52 − ₹50)₹1,800 F
VolumeStandard price × (Actual quantity − Budgeted quantity)₹50 × (900 − 1,000)₹5,000 A

Salem got ₹1,800 more from a higher price and lost ₹5,000 by selling 100 fewer. The volume loss is bigger, so the net is an adverse ₹3,200. Raising the price may well be what cut the volume.

On a profit basis. Volume is sometimes valued at the standard margin, not the price. With a standard profit of ₹20 a utensil, 100 fewer sold cost ₹2,000 of profit.

Mind the sign when you copy the cost formulas. For costs, a variance is favourable when actual is below standard, so the formula is standard minus actual. For sales it is the opposite: actual above budget is favourable, so it is actual minus standard. Some notes print the cost-style signs for sales, and that makes a lower price look favourable.

Where it breaks. The price and volume effects are linked. A higher price often lowers the volume, so each variance alone can mislead. Market conditions, not the sales team, may be the cause. For several products, a mix variance also arises.

For exams. Show the three variances and check that price plus volume equals value. State the sign rule.

Sales: actual minus standard, so above is favourable.

Go deeper for practitioners

Using the variances. A favourable price variance with an adverse volume variance suggests the firm is pricing high and losing share. The opposite points to discounting to win volume. Neither is right or wrong by itself. It depends on the margin and the capacity.

A decision. A firm raises prices by 4%, and the sales volume falls 12%. Using the contribution per unit, how would you tell whether the price rise paid?

chapters.title: Budgeting and Budgetary Control
chapters.scope: How a firm plans in numbers, links its functional budgets, and checks its results against fixed, flexible and zero-based budgets.

blocks.title: Budgeting and budgetary control
blocks.html:
A shop owner who plans nothing finds out at year-end whether she made money. One who plans can find out in March that sales are behind plan, and act in April. The plan is the budget, and the checking is control.

In plain wordsA budget is a plan for a period, in numbers. Budgetary control compares what actually happened with that plan, finds the gaps and acts on them.

Exam definitionBudgeting is the process of preparing a quantitative, monetary financial plan estimating income and expenditure for a period. Budgetary control is the continuous comparison of actual performance with budgeted figures to identify variances and take corrective action.

FunctionHow
PlanningSets financial goals for the period
CoordinationAligns the work of departments
ControlMonitors spending against the plan
Performance evaluationAssesses results against targets
Financial disciplineDirects resources to where they matter

Preparing a budget. Define the goals. Estimate income from fixed and variable sources. Classify expenses as fixed, variable and irregular. Draft the budget and allocate resources. Plan for contingencies, debt repayment and savings. Then review actual results, revise the budget when needed and keep up continuous reporting.

The control system, in order. Set objectives and the key budget factor, prepare the budgets for each department, compare actual performance with the budgets, analyse the variances, and take corrective action.

ComponentRole
Budget settingSet targets from past performance and forecasts
CommunicationTell each department its goals
ImplementationWork within the budgeted limits
Monitoring and controlCompare actual and budget, and find variances
Corrective actionInvestigate variances and revise plans

Don’t confuse budgeting with budgetary control. A budget is the plan. Budgetary control is the continuing process of checking it and acting. A budget with no control is only a forecast, and the saying goes: a budget is a plan, but control makes it work.

Where it breaks. A budget can be padded by managers who expect to be cut. It can encourage ‘spend it or lose it’. A rigid budget makes a firm slow to react when conditions change. Targets that people had no say in are often resented.

For exams. Give the two definitions, the functions, and the order of the steps in the control system. Remember the key budget factor: the one limit, often sales, that comes first.

Plan, act, compare, correct.

Go deeper for practitioners

The key budget factor. The budget for each department depends on a limit. For many firms it is sales; for a firm short of steel it is material; for one at full capacity it is plant hours. The scarce factor decides which budget is drawn up first.

A decision. A department asks for a 20% bigger budget because its actual spending last year was close to its budget. What would you ask before agreeing, and what would you propose?

blocks.title: Functional budgets and the master budget
blocks.html:
The sales team plans to sell 12,000 fans. How many must the factory make, how much material must be bought, and will there be cash to pay for it? One department’s plan sets every other department’s task.

In plain wordsEach function (sales, production, materials, cash) has its own budget. The master budget combines them into a projected profit and loss account and balance sheet.

Exam definitionA functional budget is the budget of a particular function. The sales budget estimates sales in quantity and value; the production budget determines the units to be made; the cash budget forecasts inflows and outflows; the master budget consolidates all functional budgets.

BudgetPurpose
SalesEstimates sales revenue in quantity and value; guides marketing and production
ProductionUnits to be made to meet sales and stock needs
Production costEstimates manufacturing cost: materials, labour and overheads
Materials and purchaseMaterials required, and materials to be bought for production and stock
CashForecasts inflows and outflows; ensures liquidity
PersonnelLabour costs, wages and staffing
Selling and distributionAdvertising, marketing, commission and transport
AdministrationManagement and office expenses
MasterA summary of all of them, with a projected profit and loss account and balance sheet

The production budget, worked. Tirunelveli Fans plans to sell 12,000 fans at ₹80, a sales budget of ₹9,60,000. It holds 1,500 fans at the start of the year and wants 2,000 at the end.

Units to be produced = Sales + Closing stock − Opening stock = 12,000 + 2,000 − 1,500 = 12,500

The purchase budget. Each fan needs 2 kg of material, so 12,500 fans need 25,000 kg. With 3,000 kg in stock and 4,000 kg wanted at the end, the firm must buy 25,000 + 4,000 − 3,000 = 26,000 kg.

The cash budget. There are three methods: the receipts and payments method, the adjusted profit and loss method and the balance sheet method. By the first, the firm starts with ₹50,000, expects receipts of ₹3,00,000 and payments of ₹3,20,000, and so ends with ₹30,000. If it wants a minimum of ₹40,000, the budget warns of a ₹10,000 gap, and the firm can arrange an overdraft in advance.

Don’t add the closing stock the wrong way round. Production is not sales. To end with more stock than you started with, you must make more than you sell. The formula adds the closing stock and subtracts the opening stock, and the same rule holds for materials.

Where it breaks. Everything flows from the sales budget. If sales are over-estimated, production, purchases and cash are wrong in turn, and unsold stock builds up. The master budget is only as good as its weakest forecast.

For exams. Remember the production budget formula, the three cash budget methods, and that the master budget consolidates the others.

Sales first, then production, then purchases; cash tells whether it can be paid.

Go deeper for practitioners

Cash is not profit. A firm can budget a profit and a cash shortage in the same month, if it sells on credit and buys for cash. The cash budget is the early warning, and a bank will often ask for it before agreeing an overdraft limit.

A decision. A seasonal fan-maker sells most in March to June but must make fans from November. Which budget shows the cash strain, and what could the firm do about it?

blocks.title: Fixed, flexible and zero-based budgets
blocks.html:
One manager says a plant’s costs were ₹50,000 under budget. Another says they were ₹10,000 over. Both are right, and the difference is whether the budget was adjusted for how much was actually made.

In plain wordsA fixed budget stays the same whatever the activity. A flexible budget is recalculated for the actual activity. A zero-based budget starts each year from nothing and asks every item to prove its worth.

Exam definitionA fixed budget remains unchanged irrespective of the level of activity. A flexible budget adjusts according to actual output. Zero-based budgeting requires every activity and expenditure to be justified from a zero base, with no automatic continuation of past spending.

Fixed against flexible. A plant budgets for 10,000 units at ₹30 a unit of variable cost, plus ₹1,20,000 of fixed cost, so ₹4,20,000. It makes only 8,000 units, and spends ₹3,70,000.

Fixed budgetFlexible budget
Budgeted activity10,000 units8,000 units (the actual)
Variable cost₹3,00,000₹2,40,000
Fixed cost₹1,20,000₹1,20,000
Budget allowed₹4,20,000₹3,60,000
Actual cost₹3,70,000₹3,70,000
Variance₹50,000 favourable₹10,000 adverse

The fixed budget praises a plant that made 20% fewer units. The flexible budget shows it spent ₹10,000 more than it should have for the work done.

FixedFlexible
Response to outputNone; rigidAdjusts to output
EaseSimple to prepareMore complex
Best whenConditions are stableOutput varies; for variance analysis
AccuracyPoor when actual differs from planCompares like with like

Zero-based budgeting (ZBB). Divide the organisation into decision units. Write a decision package for each, setting out its cost and benefit. Rank the packages by importance and return. Approve and fund them in rank order until the money runs out.

Don’t think zero-based means starting with no money. Zero-based means starting without assuming last year’s costs are justified. Every activity must show its case again. A useful activity usually survives, but its cost is questioned.

Where it breaks. ZBB takes a great deal of time and paperwork if done every year, and managers can overstate the benefits. Many firms use it every few years, or only for overheads. A flexible budget needs a reliable split of cost into fixed and variable.

For exams. Define each type, give two features of each and the four ZBB steps (identify decision units, develop decision packages, rank them, approve and fund).

Fixed is rigid; flexible follows the work; zero-based starts again.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why flexing matters for control. A fixed budget shows what happened against what was hoped. A flexible budget shows what happened against what should have happened for the work actually done. Only the second can fairly blame or praise a manager.

A decision. A college’s canteen cost rises every year by 8% over the last year. Where would zero-based budgeting help, and what could you ask the canteen manager to show?

chapters.title: Financial Management
chapters.scope: What financial managers decide, the objectives and functions of the role, and how projects and dividends are judged.

blocks.title: Financial management and its objectives
blocks.html:
A small garment unit in Tiruppur has orders to double its output. It must decide whether to buy machines, how to pay for them, and whether to pay the owners anything this year. These three questions are financial management.

In plain wordsFinancial management plans, organises and controls how a business raises money and puts it to use, so that the business stays healthy and grows.

Exam definitionFinancial management is the strategic planning, organising, directing and controlling of financial activities related to the procurement and utilisation of funds, to ensure the financial well-being of the enterprise.

ObjectiveKey focus
Profit maximisationIncrease financial returns for owners
Wealth maximisationIncrease the value of the business over time
Liquidity managementKeep enough cash for short-term liabilities
Risk minimisationIdentify and reduce financial risks

Why it matters. It allocates scarce resources well, supports long-term plans, keeps the firm stable through bad years, and gives it an edge over rivals that spend less carefully.

Don’t treat profit maximisation and wealth maximisation as the same. Profit maximisation looks at this year’s profit, and can be gained by cutting maintenance or taking on risk. Wealth maximisation looks at the value of the business, which also reflects the timing, size and risk of future cash flows. It is the preferred objective in most textbooks.

Where it breaks. Owners, managers, lenders and employees want different things, and it is not easy to measure ‘value’ for a firm that is not listed. A target that is too narrow, such as the quarterly profit, can harm the long-term health of the business.

For exams. Give the meaning, the four objectives, and the three decisions: investment, financing and dividend.

Where to invest, how to raise, how much to give back.

Go deeper for practitioners

Behavioural finance. Real managers and investors do not always act as the textbooks assume. Overconfidence, loss aversion and herding can push firms to over-invest in good years and under-invest in bad ones. The field studies how such habits change financial choices.

A decision. A founder-owner could take a large dividend this year or reinvest it in a new plant. Which objective is she serving in each case, and what would a minority shareholder ask?

blocks.title: Functions, scope and the role of the financial manager
blocks.html:
In a growing firm, the finance head is asked to approve a new plant, negotiate a loan, report to investors and avoid fraud, all in the same week. What is her job, and where does it end?

In plain wordsThe financial manager plans the firm’s money, raises it, puts it to work, controls it and reports on it. The scope runs from day-to-day cash to dealings in capital markets.

Exam definitionThe functions of financial management are financial planning and forecasting, investment decisions (capital budgeting), financing and capital structure management, liquidity and working capital management, risk management, dividend policy management, and financial reporting and analysis.

FunctionWhat it covers
Planning and forecastingBudgets for revenue and expenditure; forecasts of future performance
Investment decisionEvaluating projects by NPV, IRR and payback; allocating resources
Financing and capital structureThe best debt–equity mix; managing leverage
Liquidity and working capitalCash flow; managing current assets and liabilities
Risk managementIdentifying market and credit risks; hedging, insurance and diversification
Dividend policyHow much to distribute and how much to retain
Reporting and analysisFinancial statements and ratio analysis
AreaKey focus
Strategic financial managementLong-term planning of investment, financing and profit distribution
Capital marketsStock and bond markets; investor and creditor relations
Risk management and insuranceIdentifying and reducing financial risk
International financeForeign exchange risk, overseas investment and regulations
Corporate governanceTransparency, accountability and ethical compliance
Corporate restructuringMergers, acquisitions and divestitures
Behavioural financePsychological factors in financial decisions
Tax managementTax planning and legal compliance

The role of the financial manager. Strategic planning and decision-making; raising capital and managing investors; monitoring and control through budgets, variance analysis and internal controls; investor relations; advising senior management; and ensuring compliance and ethical practice.

Don’t confuse the financial manager with the accountant. The accountant records and reports what has happened. The financial manager uses that information to decide what to do next: which projects, what funding, and what risks. The two roles work closely, and in small firms may be one person.

Where it breaks. A financial manager can be overruled by owners, and can be pressed to show good numbers for lenders. Internal controls reduce the risk of fraud but do not remove it. The role also expects judgement under uncertainty, which no formula supplies.

For exams. Learn the seven functions as a list, the three decisions, and the main duties of the financial manager.

Plan, invest, fund, keep liquid, cover risk, pay out, report.

Go deeper for practitioners

Working capital as daily finance. Of the seven functions, liquidity is the one that fails first. A profitable firm can stop functioning for want of cash. The ratios of Chapter 4 and the cash budget of Chapter 12 are the working tools of the liquidity function.

A decision. A company has surplus cash for three months before a big payment is due. What would the financial manager weigh in deciding where to place it?

blocks.title: Capital budgeting and dividend policy
blocks.html:
A firm can buy a machine for ₹10 lakh that will earn ₹4 lakh a year for four years. Is it worth it? The ₹16 lakh is spread over time, and money in four years is worth less than money now. Capital budgeting gives three ways to judge.

In plain wordsCapital budgeting judges long-term projects by comparing what they cost now with what they bring in later. Dividend policy decides how much of the profit goes to the owners and how much stays in the business.

Exam definitionCapital budgeting is the process of evaluating and selecting long-term investment projects using tools such as net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR) and payback period.
