Dividend policy is management’s decision on the proportion of profit distributed as dividends versus retained.

MethodWhat it isDecision rule
Payback periodTime to recover the initial outlay from the cash inflowsAccept if within a set period
Net present value (NPV)Sum of discounted inflows less the initial outlayAccept if positive
Internal rate of return (IRR)The discount rate at which NPV is zeroAccept if it exceeds the required return

Worked example. A machine costs ₹10,00,000 and brings in ₹4,00,000 a year for 4 years. The firm’s cost of capital is 12%.

Payback = ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000 = 2.5 years
NPV = ₹4,00,000 × (annuity factor for 12%, 4 years: 3.0373) − ₹10,00,000, which is about ₹2,14,900
IRR ≈ 21.9%: the rate at which ₹4,00,000 for 4 years is worth exactly ₹10,00,000

All three say accept: payback is short, NPV is positive, and the IRR of 21.9% is well above the required 12%. A weaker machine bringing in only ₹2,80,000 a year has an NPV of about −₹1,49,500 at 12%, and would be rejected.

Dividend policy. Under the residual theory, a firm first funds every acceptable project from profits and pays out only what remains. If it earns ₹10,00,000 and good projects need ₹6,00,000, the dividend is ₹4,00,000, a payout of 40%. Under the relevance view, the dividend itself affects the value of the firm, because investors like steady, certain income.

Don’t rely on payback alone. Payback ignores cash flows after the recovery date and ignores the time value of money. A project with a quick payback but few later returns can look better than one that pays back slowly but earns for twenty years. Use NPV as the main test.

Where it breaks. All the methods rest on forecast cash flows, which are uncertain. A small change in the discount rate or the forecast can flip the result. The IRR can mislead when projects differ in size or have uneven cash flows, and NPV and IRR can then rank projects differently.

For exams. Remember the decision rules, the link to the cost of capital (Chapter 15), and the two dividend theories.

Positive NPV adds value; IRR above the cost of capital agrees.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why the discount rate is the cost of capital. A project must earn at least what its funds cost, or the firm loses value by undertaking it. That is why the WACC of Chapter 15 is the discount rate for NPV and the hurdle rate for IRR.

A decision. Two projects need the same outlay. One pays ₹5 lakh in year one and nothing after. The other pays ₹2 lakh a year for five years. The firm’s cost of capital is 15%. How would you choose, and what does payback hide?

text: The Īśa Upaniṣad opens by saying that all of this is pervaded by the divine, and advises enjoying through renunciation, without coveting anyone’s wealth. A financial manager handles money that belongs to others. The text speaks of wealth in general and not of a firm’s funds, so the link to stewardship of other people’s money is a reading.
pairings.quote: ईशावास्यमिदं सर्वम् … मा गृधः कस्य स्विद्धनम् । īśāvāsyam idaṃ sarvam… mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam. Īśa Upaniṣad 1

chapters.title: Sources of Finance
chapters.scope: How the money for a business is classified, and the main owned, borrowed, long-term and short-term sources.

blocks.title: Classifying sources of finance
blocks.html:
A tea-estate owner needs ₹50 lakh: ₹30 lakh for new machinery to last twenty years and ₹20 lakh to buy leaf and pay wages for the next three months. Using one source for both would be a mistake. The first step is to sort the sources.

In plain wordsSources of finance can be sorted five ways: by how long the money is needed, who provides it, where it comes from, what it is used for, and whether it changes who controls the firm.

Exam definitionSources of finance are classified on the basis of time period (long, medium, short), ownership (owned, borrowed), source of generation (internal, external), nature of financing (fixed capital, working capital) and ownership and control (internal and external ownership sources).

BasisClassesExamples
Time periodLong-term (over 5 years); medium-term (1 to 5 years); short-term (up to 1 year)Shares, debentures, retained profit; term loans, leases; trade credit, overdraft
OwnershipOwned capital; borrowed capitalEquity and preference shares, retained profit; debentures, loans, deposits
Source of generationInternal; externalRetained profit, sale of assets, depreciation funds; shares, debentures, bank loans
Nature of financingFixed capital; working capitalLand, building, machinery; stock, wages, rent, bills
Ownership and controlInternal ownership sources; external ownership sourcesRetained earnings and reserves; new shares, institutional loans

Matching. A good rule is to match the life of the funds with the life of the need. Machinery that lasts twenty years is financed with long-term funds, and leaf stock with short-term ones. Financing a long-term asset with short-term funds forces a refinancing each year, and is risky.

Owned capitalBorrowed capital
Who provides itOwners or shareholdersOutsiders
RepaymentNone; permanentRepayable with interest
ReturnDividend or profit share; not fixedFixed interest
ControlGives ownership rightsGives no ownership rights
Risk to the firmLower: no fixed chargeHigher: interest due whether or not there is profit

Don’t think ‘external’ always means ‘borrowed’. A new issue of equity shares is an external source, but it is owned capital, not borrowed. The two classifications ask different questions: where the money comes from, and who has a claim on it.

Where it breaks. The time limits are conventions, and books differ. A debenture can be medium-term, and a bank loan can be short, medium or long. Preference shares are called owned capital but carry a fixed dividend and are redeemable, so they sit between owned and borrowed capital.

For exams. Know the five bases and one example for each class, and the difference between owned and borrowed capital.

Time, ownership, origin, nature, control.

Go deeper for practitioners

Internal finance first. Retained profit has no issue cost, no new shareholders and no repayment date, which is why many firms prefer it. The pecking order theory of Chapter 16 builds on this. The catch is that it is limited by how much profit the firm earns, and shareholders forgo dividends.

A decision. A bakery wants to open a second shop costing ₹15 lakh. List which of the five classifications each possible source falls into, and which you would pick.

blocks.title: Owned sources: equity, preference and retained earnings
blocks.html:
A founder wants outside money but does not want to be tied to a repayment date. She can sell a share in the business. In return, she gives up some control and some of the profit.

In plain wordsOwned capital is money from the owners. It has no repayment date, and it carries the first risk of loss and the last claim on profit.

Exam definitionEquity shares represent ownership in the company, with voting rights and dividends that vary with profit. Preference shares carry a fixed dividend and preference over equity in dividend and repayment, usually without voting rights. Retained earnings are profits reinvested rather than distributed.

SourceFeaturesCost and risk
Equity sharesLong-term, owned, external; voting rights and variable dividend; unlimited upsideHigh risk for the holder; no repayment burden for the firm
Preference sharesLong-term, owned, external; fixed dividend; paid before equity in dividend and repayment; usually no voteA hybrid of equity and debt; the dividend is fixed, and on cumulative shares unpaid dividends carry forward
Retained earningsLong-term, owned, internal; profits ploughed backGenerally low cost to raise; has an opportunity cost, the dividend forgone

For the firm. Equity gives permanent funds and no fixed charges, but dilutes control and is the costliest source. Preference shares give funds without sharing votes, but the dividend is fixed. Retained earnings need no issue and no outsiders, but are limited to what is earned.

Reserves. A part of profit may be kept in reserves, such as a general reserve. Retained earnings and reserves are internal ownership sources, because they come from the firm’s own profit and do not dilute control.

Don’t call preference shares debt. Preference shares are shares: the dividend is paid out of profit, not as a tax-deductible interest cost, and holders are not creditors. They rank before equity but after debt on winding up. That in-between position is why past exam papers call them a hybrid.

Where it breaks. Equity issued in a bad market sells cheap, and dilutes existing owners more. Retained profit is not free: shareholders could have earned a return by investing the dividend themselves. A firm that keeps too much can be seen as hoarding.

For exams. Remember the features and the nature of each: long-term, owned, with the external or internal tag.

Equity shares the risk, preference shares the order, retention shares nothing.

Go deeper for practitioners

Cumulative and redeemable. A cumulative preference share carries unpaid dividends forward, so none can be paid to equity until they are cleared. A redeemable one has a repayment date, which makes it more like debt. Companies law governs the types a company may issue, so check the current Act.

A decision. A family-owned firm needs ₹2 crore and wants to keep control. Which of the three owned sources suits it, and what would it give up?

blocks.title: Borrowed sources and short-term finance
blocks.html:
A trader has sold goods worth ₹1,00,000 on a bill payable in three months, but needs cash today. Waiting is not an option. A bank can pay now, for a fee, and that is only one of many ways to borrow.

In plain wordsBorrowed finance is money that must be repaid with interest. Short-term sources keep a business running day to day; long-term ones fund assets.

Exam definitionBorrowed sources include debentures and bonds, bank loans, public deposits, trade credit, bills discounting, lease financing, hire purchase, commercial paper and factoring. Their holders are creditors, not owners.

SourceTermKey features
Debentures and bondsLongFixed-rate, repayable; holders are creditors, not owners
Bank loansShort, medium or longFlexible repayment and interest; secured or unsecured
Public depositsMedium (1 to 5 years)Accepted from the public for a fixed term; often unsecured
Trade creditShortSuppliers allow purchase now and payment later
Bills discountingShortA bill is sold to a bank at a discount before it is due
Lease financingMedium or longRight to use an asset for rent; ownership does not pass
Hire purchaseMediumAsset bought by instalments; ownership passes after the last payment
Commercial paperShortAn unsecured promissory note, issued by large firms
FactoringShortReceivables sold to a financial institution for immediate cash

Bills discounting, worked. A bank discounts a ₹1,00,000 bill with 3 months to run at 12% a year. The discount is ₹1,00,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹3,000, so the trader gets ₹97,000 now. The true yearly cost on the money received is 12.4%, slightly more than 12%, since the interest is deducted at the start.

Lease against hire purchase. A lessee uses an asset for rent and the lessor keeps the ownership, and usually the tax claim for depreciation. A hire purchaser pays by instalments and becomes the owner after the last one, and generally claims the depreciation and the interest. Tax treatment can change, so check the current rules.

Trade credit is not free. Terms of ‘2/10 net 30’ mean a 2% discount for paying in 10 days, otherwise the full amount in 30. Skipping the discount costs about 37% a year, so a firm that uses the full credit period is borrowing at a very high rate.

Don’t treat debentures as shares. A debenture holder lends money and is owed interest whether or not there is profit. A shareholder owns part of the firm. Interest on debentures is a tax-deductible cost; dividends are not.

Where it breaks. Borrowing adds fixed obligations. Too much short-term borrowing to fund long-term assets can leave a firm unable to renew the loans. Factoring and discounting can signal that a firm is short of cash. Check the conditions on security, covenants and the rate.

For exams. Know each source’s term and main feature, the lease and hire purchase difference, and the description of commercial paper and factoring.

Match the life of the money to the life of the need.

Go deeper for practitioners

Cost of the cheapest-looking source. Trade credit seems free, bank overdraft seems flexible, and a lease seems to need no capital. Each has a hidden price: a lost discount, a floating rate, or a lock-in. A firm should compare the full cost, which is the subject of the next chapter.

A decision. A wholesaler is offered 2/10 net 30 terms. She can borrow from a bank at 14%. Should she take the discount by borrowing, and why?

chapters.title: Cost of Capital
chapters.scope: What it costs a firm to raise money, how each source is priced, and how the weighted average sets the hurdle for new projects.

blocks.title: The cost of capital
blocks.html:
A bank lends at 10%. Shareholders expect more than that for taking the greater risk. A firm that earns less than it costs to raise its money loses value, even if its profit is positive. So what does the money cost?

In plain wordsThe cost of capital is the return investors need in order to supply money to the firm. If a project earns less than this, the firm is worse off.

Exam definitionThe cost of capital is the required rate of return expected by providers of finance for supplying funds to a business. It is the minimum return a firm must earn on its investments to satisfy investors and maintain its market value.

TypeMeaning
Explicit costThe actual cost paid for raising capital, such as interest or dividends
Implicit costThe opportunity cost of using funds, such as earnings kept back
Specific costThe cost of one source of finance, such as debt or equity
Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)The average cost of all sources, weighted by their proportions
Marginal cost of capital (MCC)The cost of the next increment of capital raised
FactorEffect
Risk profileHigher business or financial risk leads to a higher required return
Capital structureDebt may lower the cost, up to an optimal point
Dividend policyHigher dividends may increase reliance on external funds
Tax rateA higher tax rate raises the interest tax shield and lowers the after-tax cost of debt
Market conditionsInterest rates and investor expectations affect the cost of finance
CreditworthinessA better credit rating lowers the borrowing cost

Risk and return. The riskier the investment, the higher the return investors expect, and the higher the cost of capital. A safe lender asks for less than an equity holder.

Why it matters. It is the discount rate for NPV and IRR (Chapter 13). It guides the choice of debt and equity (Chapter 16). It informs the dividend decision, and the valuation of shares, bonds and whole firms.

Don’t think retained earnings are free. Retained profit has no interest and no issue cost, but shareholders could have used the dividend elsewhere. That forgone return is an implicit cost, and it is why the cost of retained earnings is taken as about equal to the cost of equity.

Where it breaks. The cost of equity cannot be seen in a bill; it has to be estimated, and each method (dividend growth, earnings yield, CAPM) gives a different answer. A cost of capital for the whole firm can be wrong for a project that is much riskier than the firm’s usual business.

For exams. Know the types, the factors, the significance for the four financial decisions, and the rule: accept projects earning more than the cost of capital.

Risk up, required return up, cost of capital up.

Go deeper for practitioners

A project-specific rate. A firm that makes tyres and starts an overseas venture should not use its tyre WACC for the new business. The venture’s own risk sets the right discount rate, which may be higher.

A decision. Two firms in the same trade have the same debt, but one has a better credit rating. Whose cost of capital is lower, and what difference does that make to the projects each can accept?

blocks.title: Specific costs: debt, preference, equity and retained earnings
blocks.html:
Before averaging the costs of different sources, each one has to be priced alone. Debt has a visible interest rate, and equity has no rate at all. The formulas bridge the gap.

In plain wordsEach source has its own cost: debt after tax, preference on its fixed dividend, and equity estimated from what shareholders expect. Retained earnings cost about the same as equity.

Exam definitionCost of debt Kd = I(1 − T) ÷ NP. Cost of preference capital Kp = Dp ÷ NP. Cost of equity Ke may be estimated by the dividend growth model D1 ÷ P0 + g, the earnings yield E1 ÷ P0, or CAPM: Rf + β(Rm − Rf). Cost of retained earnings Kr ≈ Ke.

SourceFormulaWhere
Debt (before tax)Kd = I ÷ NPI = interest, NP = net proceeds
Debt (after tax)Kd = I(1 − T) ÷ NPT = tax rate
PreferenceKp = Dp ÷ NPDp = preference dividend
Equity: dividend growthKe = D1 ÷ P0 + gD1 = next dividend, P0 = price, g = growth
Equity: earnings yieldKe = E1 ÷ P0E1 = expected earnings per share
Equity: CAPMKe = Rf + β(Rm − Rf)Rf = risk-free return, β = beta, Rm = market return
Retained earningsKr ≈ KeOpportunity cost to shareholders

Worked examples (tax rate 25%).

Debt: a ₹100 debenture at 10% interest, with net proceeds of ₹95. Before tax Kd = 10 ÷ 95 = 10.53%. After tax Kd = 10 × (1 − 0.25) ÷ 95 = 7.89%
Preference: ₹100 share at 12%, net proceeds ₹96. Kp = 12 ÷ 96 = 12.5%
Equity, dividend growth: next dividend ₹6, price ₹100, growth 4%. Ke = 6 ÷ 100 + 0.04 = 10%
Equity, earnings yield: expected earnings ₹10 on a ₹100 share. Ke = 10 ÷ 100 = 10%
Equity, CAPM: risk-free 7%, β = 1.2, market return 12%. Ke = 7 + 1.2 × (12 − 7) = 13%

The three estimates of equity cost differ because they assume different things. CAPM includes the share’s own risk through beta, while the dividend growth model needs a reliable forecast of growth.

Don’t use the pre-tax interest rate in WACC. Interest is tax-deductible, so the firm bears only the after-tax cost. Preference dividends and equity dividends are paid from profit after tax, and do not get a tax saving. Using 10% where 7.9% belongs overstates the cost of debt.

Where it breaks. Net proceeds are the price less issue costs and discount, so they change the cost. The dividend growth model fails for a firm that pays no dividend. CAPM depends on a good beta and a market risk premium, and neither is certain. The earnings yield ignores growth.

For exams. Learn each formula and what each symbol stands for, and use net proceeds, not the face value, as the denominator.

Debt after tax, preference on net proceeds, equity by one of three routes.

Go deeper for practitioners

Beta. A beta above 1 means the share moves more than the market, and so demands a higher return. A beta below 1 means it moves less. A defensive firm such as a power utility has a low beta, and a fast-growing technology firm a high one.

A decision. Your three estimates of Ke are 10%, 10% and 13%. Which would you use for a firm that pays regular dividends, and which for a start-up that pays none?

blocks.title: Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
blocks.html:
A firm has borrowed some money, issued preference shares and used equity, each at a different cost. A single rate is needed to judge a project, and that is the average, weighted by how much each source supplies.

In plain wordsWACC is the average cost of all the money in the firm, where each source counts in proportion to how much of the total it supplies.

Exam definitionWACC = wdKd + wpKp + weKe + wrKr, where the w are the weights of debt, preference, equity and retained earnings in the capital structure and the K are their costs. It is the minimum average return that investors require.

WACC = (weight of debt × cost of debt) + (weight of preference × cost of preference) + (weight of equity × cost of equity)

Worked example. A firm has debt of ₹2,00,000 costing 10%, preference capital of ₹50,000 costing 12%, and equity of ₹2,50,000 costing 15%. The costs are taken after tax.

SourceAmountCostWeightWeighted cost
Debt₹2,00,00010%0.404%
Preference₹50,00012%0.101.2%
Equity₹2,50,00015%0.507.5%
Total₹5,00,0001.0012.7%
WACC = 4.0% + 1.2% + 7.5% = 12.7%

The decision rule. A project earning more than the WACC creates value, and one earning less destroys it. A project that returns 14% will add value for this firm, and one that returns 11% will not.

Marginal cost of capital. The WACC describes the money already raised. The marginal cost of capital is the cost of the next rupee, which can be higher once cheap sources are used up, for example when the firm has used all its retained earnings and must issue new shares.

Don’t use book values and market values as if they were the same. Weights can be taken at book value (as above, from the balance sheet) or at market value. Market values are better, because they show what investors currently demand, but they are harder to obtain for debt and unlisted firms. State which you use.

Where it breaks. The weights change as the firm raises new money, so the WACC changes too. The result depends on the cost estimates, which are uncertain, especially for equity. Using one firm-wide rate for projects of very different risk can lead to wrong accept or reject decisions.

For exams. Show the table with source, amount, cost, weight and weighted cost, and a total of weights equal to 1.

Weight each cost by its share, then add.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why debt lowers the WACC, up to a point. Debt is cheaper than equity because it is safer for the lender and the interest saves tax. Adding it lowers the average. But more debt raises the risk to shareholders and so the cost of equity, and in time the cost of debt as well. The theories of the next chapter disagree on how far this goes.

A decision. A project returns 13% and the WACC is 12.7%, but the project is far riskier than the firm’s usual business. Should the firm accept it, and what rate would you use instead?

chapters.title: Capital Structure Theories
chapters.scope: Whether the mix of debt and equity changes a firm’s value: the net income, net operating income and Modigliani–Miller theories, and the trade-off, pecking order, agency and market-timing explanations.

blocks.title: Net income and net operating income theories
blocks.html:
A firm’s earnings before interest and tax are the same whether it is funded by owners or by lenders. Does the mix of funding change what the firm is worth? Two early theories give opposite answers.

In plain wordsThe net income (NI) theory says that more debt always makes the firm more valuable. The net operating income (NOI) theory says the mix makes no difference to value.

Exam definitionThe net income approach assumes the cost of equity Ke and the cost of debt Kd are constant and Kd is lower than Ke, so a rise in leverage lowers the overall cost of capital Ko and raises the value of the firm. The net operating income approach assumes Ko is constant and the value of the firm is V = EBIT ÷ Ko whatever the leverage.

The firm. It earns an EBIT of ₹6,00,000. It can raise ₹20,00,000 of debt at 10%, with interest of ₹2,00,000 a year.

No debtDebt of ₹20,00,000
EBIT₹6,00,000₹6,00,000
InterestNil₹2,00,000
Earnings for equity₹6,00,000₹4,00,000
Value of equity = Earnings ÷ 15%₹40,00,000₹26,66,667
Value of debtNil₹20,00,000
Value of the firm₹40,00,000₹46,66,667
Overall cost of capital Ko = EBIT ÷ Value15%12.9%

Debt lowers Ko from 15% to 12.9% and raises the value of the firm by about ₹6.7 lakh. Carried to its end, the theory says a firm should be funded wholly by debt.

No debtDebt of ₹20,00,000
Value of the firm = EBIT ÷ 12%₹50,00,000₹50,00,000
Value of debtNil₹20,00,000
Value of equity₹50,00,000₹30,00,000
Earnings for equity₹6,00,000₹4,00,000
Cost of equity Ke = Earnings ÷ Equity12%13.3%

In the NOI view, cheap debt is offset by a rising cost of equity: shareholders see more risk and ask for more, from 12% to 13.3%. Debt up, Ke up, Ko constant, value constant.

The logic of the NI theory, in order. Ke and Kd are assumed constant. Debt is cheaper than equity, so more leverage reduces the overall cost of capital. A lower cost of capital raises the value of the firm. So value is maximised by using as much debt as possible.

Don’t treat the NI and NOI theories as findings. They are assumptions about how investors behave. The NI theory assumes shareholders do not mind extra risk from debt; the NOI theory assumes they mind it exactly enough to cancel the saving. Neither is proved, and the next theory tests both.

Where it breaks. No real firm borrows 100% of its capital, so the NI conclusion fails: lenders raise their rates and shareholders ask more. The NOI view ignores tax and the cost of financial distress. Real firms lie in between, which led to the traditional (intermediate) view.

For exams. Remember: NI: debt up, WACC down, value up. NOI: debt up, Ke up, Ko constant, value constant. V = EBIT ÷ Ko under NOI.

NI: more debt, more value. NOI: more debt, same value.

Go deeper for practitioners

The traditional view. A middle theory holds that moderate debt lowers the cost of capital because it is cheap, but past some point rising risk overtakes the saving, so there is an optimal structure. The trade-off theory, in the third concept, gives that a reason.

A decision. A lender says it will charge 10% up to ₹20 lakh and 14% beyond. Which of NI or NOI is closer to reality in that case, and why?

blocks.title: Modigliani–Miller and leverage irrelevance
blocks.html:
The NOI theory says the mix does not matter, but gives only an assumption. In 1958 Modigliani and Miller proved it, under strict conditions, by showing that if a firm’s value did depend on its debt, traders could make a risk-free profit.

In plain wordsIn a perfect market without taxes, a firm’s value depends on its operating earnings and risk, not on how it is funded. Once taxes exist, debt adds value through the interest tax shield.

Exam definitionProposition I: in a perfect market with no taxes, VL = VU. Proposition II: the cost of equity rises with leverage, Ke = Ko + (Ko − Kd) × D/E. With corporate taxes, interest is deductible and VL = VU + T × D.

Proposition II, checked. Take the NOI firm: Ko = 12%, Kd = 10%, debt ₹20,00,000 and equity ₹30,00,000, so D/E = 0.67.

Ke = 12% + (12% − 10%) × 0.67 = 13.3%

It matches the 13.3% found from the earnings. The extra return that shareholders ask is exactly the compensation for the risk that debt adds, so the overall cost stays at 12%.

Homemade leverage. Suppose an investor wants the return of a levered share but only unlevered shares exist. With ₹1,00,000 of her own, she borrows ₹66,667 at 10% and buys ₹1,66,667 of the unlevered firm, a 3.33% stake. Her share of the earnings is 3.33% of ₹6,00,000, or ₹20,000. After interest of ₹6,667, she keeps ₹13,333 on ₹1,00,000, a return of 13.3%. That is exactly the cost of equity of the levered firm.

Because investors can create leverage for themselves, they will not pay extra for a firm that does it for them. This is the leverage irrelevance argument: financing mix does not affect value, WACC stays constant at every debt-equity ratio, and value depends on earnings and asset risk.

Without taxesWith taxes
Capital structureIrrelevant to firm valueDebt adds value through the interest tax shield
ValueVL = VUVL = VU + T × D
Cost of equityRises with leverage, as aboveStill rises with leverage, but the tax shield adds value

The tax shield. At a 25% tax rate and ₹20,00,000 of permanent debt, the shield is 25% × ₹20,00,000 = ₹5,00,000. The levered firm is worth ₹50,00,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹55,00,000.

Don’t read M–M as saying debt is harmless. M–M says that in a world with no taxes, no bankruptcy costs and no information gaps, the mix does not matter. It is a benchmark that shows what must be added to explain real behaviour: taxes, distress costs and agency costs.

Where it breaks. People cannot borrow as cheaply as large firms, and markets are not frictionless. Bankruptcy costs money, and a firm near distress loses customers and suppliers. The tax-shield model, taken alone, would also call for nearly 100% debt, which is not seen in practice.

For exams. State both propositions, the formula for Ke, the effect of tax, and what homemade leverage means.

Without taxes: irrelevant. With taxes: debt gives a shield.

Go deeper for practitioners

Value and the cost of capital. In the no-tax case, Ko does not fall as debt rises, because the cheap debt is exactly offset by the dearer equity. With tax, the after-tax cost of debt is lower and Ko does fall, which is why the shield adds value.

A decision. A firm’s owners say, ‘debt is cheap at 10%, equity costs 15%, so using more debt must lower our cost of capital.’ Using Proposition II, explain what is missing from their reasoning.

blocks.title: Trade-off, pecking order, agency cost and market timing
blocks.html:
In practice, real firms are neither all-debt nor all-equity. Textbooks offer four reasons for the mix that firms choose, and each says something true about how managers behave.

In plain wordsFour theories explain real financing choices: firms weigh the tax benefit of debt against the cost of distress, prefer internal funds first, use debt to discipline managers, and time the issue of shares to the market.

Exam definitionTrade-off theory balances the tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress. Pecking order theory (Myers and Majluf) holds that firms prefer internal funds, then debt, then new equity. Agency cost theory weighs the discipline of debt against monitoring costs. Market timing theory holds that firms issue equity when it is overvalued.

TheoryCentral ideaMemory cue
Trade-offTax benefits of debt, set against financial distress costs, give an optimal ratio where marginal benefit equals marginal costTax benefit ↔ distress costs
Pecking orderBecause managers know more than outsiders, firms use retained earnings first, then debt, and new equity lastInternal funds → debt → equity
Agency costDebt’s fixed payments discipline managers, but monitoring, covenants and risk-shifting add costsDebt discipline ↔ agency conflicts
Market timingFirms issue equity when they think it is overvalued, and repurchase shares or use debt when they think it is undervaluedMarket conditions → financing choice

Trade-off. Debt gives a tax shield, but the more a firm borrows the greater the chance and cost of distress: lost customers, forced asset sales and lawyers’ fees. The best mix is where one more rupee of debt adds as much cost as benefit.

Pecking order. A new share issue signals to outsiders that managers think the shares are overpriced, so it lowers the price. Retained earnings avoid that signal, and debt sends a milder one. This explains why profitable firms often carry little debt: they do not need to borrow.

Agency costs. Managers may waste free cash. Fixed interest takes cash out of their hands, and so can improve discipline. But lenders then add covenants and monitoring, and shareholders of a heavily indebted firm may take extra risks at the lenders’ expense.

Market timing. A firm that sells shares when prices are high, and buys them back when low, ends up with a mix that reflects the history of the market. The theory explains why debt-equity ratios drift over time, rather than settling at a target.

Don’t treat these as rival answers. They answer different questions. Trade-off and agency theories give a target ratio. Pecking order and market timing describe the order and timing of choices. A firm may follow a target ratio loosely while using the pecking order day to day.

Where it breaks. None of them predicts every firm. Pecking order fits large firms better than small ones, and trade-off has trouble explaining why some profitable firms use so little debt. Market timing is hard to separate from luck.

For exams. Know the central idea and the cue for each of the seven theories (these four, with NI, NOI and M–M), and the order of the pecking order.

Trade off the shield, peck from inside, discipline with debt, time the market.

Go deeper for practitioners

Putting it together. A growing technology start-up has few assets to pledge and high distress costs, so trade-off says little debt. A mature utility with steady cash and tax to shield can carry much more. Pecking order says both prefer retained earnings first.

A decision. A family-run firm has no outside shareholders and a very trustworthy manager. Which of the four theories matters least to it, and which most?

text: Kauṭilya assumes that officials who handle funds will find it hard not to take some, and prescribes audits, rotation of posts and an accounts office. Agency cost theory makes the same assumption about managers, and holds that fixed debt payments discipline them. The text is about the king’s officials, not company managers, so the link to capital structure is a reading.
